PREFACE TO SECOND EDITION 

The law of Mortgages during the last ten years has been developed to a considerable extent in the trial of cases involving this subject, and the Statutes of Michigan have been greatly modified in relation to Mortgages, and it is believed that a revised edition of this work will be of advantage to the profession. 

Encouraged by the reception with which the first edition of this book has been met I have revised the same, adding references to recent statutes and adjudicated cases.

While the text is generally applicable to the subject of Mortgages, for the purpose of keeping the work within bounds that will not make it prohibitive as a text book for law students, I have made few references to cases in other states than the State of Michigan. 

Inasmuch as the practice in relation to the Foreclosure of Land Contracts has had a tendency to follow the practice of Foreclosure of Mortgages, I have added a chapter in relation to this subject. I have not gone into the subject of land contracts fully, as in the main such a discussion would be foreign to the subject of Mortgages.

February 1, 1933 FRED H. ALDRICH 1 iii

PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION 

The need of a concise statement of the law of Mortgages applicable particularly to the State of Michigan has often been discussed by the practitioners of this state.

This work was prepared for the use of students in law schools and by somewhat amplifying the lectures upon which the same is based, and adding notes and forms, it is hoped that it will meet the needs of the profession. FRED H. ALDRICH June 1, 1923

I. EARLY USE OF MORTGAGES. 

§1. Derivation Unknown. It would be impossible to tell at what time mortgages were first used in that system of laws of which ours forms a part, or in any of those systems which have to a greater or less extent affected those from which the American system derives its source. 

It is certain that in times of which the Bible makes a record something in the nature of a mortgage was known. 

The Roman hypotheca laws refer to something that corresponds with our present ideas of a mortgage.¹ The 

18tory's Equity Jurisprudence, 

Sec. 1206. 1

§ 2] 

early institutions of all civilized peoples had methods of securing the repayment of indebtedness that have something in common with the mortgage as it is known in this country. 

§ 2. At Common Law. At common law the legal estate vested in the mortgagee and was forfeited upon default. Equity established the right of redemption after default. From these principles is derived the doctrine of mortgages as it exists at the present time in England and in a large part of our own country. § 3. Tendency to Change from Legal to Equitable 

Theory. There has been a tendency to change from the legal to the equitable theory of mortgages. Under this theory, the title to the property vests in the mortgagor, and the mortgagee has an interest which is a chattel interest, and the "equity of redemption" in the mortgagor is a term which is construed to represent the legal interest. The mortgagor has title in the property subject to the mortgage prior to default as well as a right to pay the mortgage within a certain time after default. 

The term "equity of redemption" thus used is not a perfectly accurate expression. It implies a right to redeem after the title has been lost, and is founded upon the ancient doctrine that the title to the property mortgaged was in the mortgagee, and that the mortgagor had an equitable right to redeem the property from the effect of the mortgage.³

I. GENERAL STATEMENT. 

89. No Particular Form Necessary. It has been usually supposed that the statute providing for short forms

FORM AND ESSENTIALS OF A MORTGAGE [§ 12 

of deeds and mortgages is entirely modern in its origin, but Chancellor Kent observes: "I apprehend that a deed would be perfectly competent in any part of the United States to convey the fee if it was to be in the following effect: I, A. B., in consideration of one dollar to me paid by C. D., do bargain and sell (or in New York, grant) to

C. D. and his heirs (in New York, Va., etc., his heirs may be omitted) the land…………. (described). "Witness my hand and seal, etc." §10. Sufficiency as to Form. Stated in a general way, any instrument which, in form conveys real estate, the purpose of which is to give to the grantee security for an indebtedness is, under our laws, a mortgage.¹ Thus a deed in trust to secure a debt is in legal effect a mortgage, even if the same does not contain a clause providing that it shall be void upon the contingency of the payment of such debt, and a deed absolute upon its face, but intended to be merely a security for a debt, is regarded in equity as a mortgage. 

§ 11. Construction Under Michigan Statutes. It is provided in Michigan Statutes that "no mortgage shall be construed as implying a covenant for the payment of the sum thereby intended to be secured, and where there shall be no express covenant for such payment contained in the mortgage, and no bond or other separate instrument to secure such payment shall have been given, the remedies of the mortgagee shall be confined to the lands mentioned in the mortgage."

II. FORMAL PARTS OF THE INSTRUMENT. 

§ 12. Description of Parties. The parties should be described accurately, and in the preparation of a mortgage, the grantors' names should be written in the same 

1 Flint & P. M. Ry. Co. v. Audi tor General, 41 Mich. 635. case cited in Sec. 8.

manner as their names were written in the instrument by which they acquired title to the property. This may not be necessary to the validity of the instrument, but such a course avoids confusion, and in many instances prevents litigation. 

§ 13. The Consideration. The consideration should be recited, although such recitation is not necessary to the validity of the instrument if it is actually founded upon a valid consideration. 

§14. Description of Premises. The premises should be accurately described. A court of equity will reform a description in case of fraud or mutual mistake, but very strong proof is required to support an allegation that by mistake a mortgage was made to embrace lands that ought not to have been put in where the person complaining of the mistake is the mortgagor who actually owned the property included at the time that the mortgage was made.¹

It has been held in certain instances that a mortgage describing land by township and range without stating in what county or state the land was situated is void, but the courts take special notice of government surveys and legal subdivisions, and when the state and county are not named, will generally presume that the land is situated in the state where the parties reside."

§ 17. Note and Mortgage Construed Together. The note and mortgage are construed as if they were parts of one instrument and in relation to the same subject as parts of one transaction constituting one contract. 

When the provisions of a note differ from those of a mortgage concerning payment, etc., the provisions of the note control.⁹ 

§18. Rule as to Interest on Past Due Mortgage. In different states the rule as to interest upon mortgages past due differs. In Michigan the interest stipulated for in the instrument governs until decree and thereafter.10 

IV. STIPULATIONS CONCERNING DEFAULT. 

§19. Acceleration of Time of Payment. A stipulation that the whole sum shall become due and payable upon any default of the payment on the principal or interest is held to be legal and valid. After the mortgagee has elected to declare the whole amount due by reason of a default, under such a clause in a mortgage he cannot be compelled to take the amount which would have been

§ 20. Partial Release. Often stipulations are made in mortgages providing that a portion of the mortgaged premises may be released upon the payment of a part of the principal upon such mortgage, providing no default has been made at the time when such release is sought. 

This clause will be enforced according to its terms, and if any default existed at the time release was sought, the mortgagee could refuse to release any part of the premises under such provision.

A covenant in a mortgage for a release of a part of mortgaged land upon the payment of a stipulated sum runs with the land. The mortgagee of the grantee of mortgaged land is entitled under the covenant in the original mortgage for the release of a part of the land upon the payment of a stipulated sum, to the release of the land covered by the second mortgage upon payment of such sum.11a

A provision in a mortgage covering about 6,000 acres of land for the release of "any of the parcels of land herein described containing 40 acres or any multiple thereof," on the payment of $2.50 per acre, is construed as establishing the government 40 acre parcel, whether full or fractional, as a unit, in order to permit releases of any of the premises in such units or combination of units, and to not allow the splitting of a unit singly or in combination with others.11b

I. IN GENeral. 

§ 31. Who May Give or Take a Mortgage. In general, any person who has legal capacity to act for himself may mortgage his property, may authorize anyone else to do this in his behalf, or may take a mortgage. By statutory provisions in many states, guardians or others acting for infants, insane or other persons without legal 16

[§ capacity to act for themselves, may be authorized by a court upon showing sufficient cause, to convey in mortgage the real estate of their wards. The jurisdiction of a court to order the mortgaging of a decedent's real estate can only be exercised in the manner and by the procedure prescribed by the statute.¹ 

§ 32. Mortgage by Guardian, Executor, etc. In all instances where a mortgage is made by a guardian, executor or administrator, the statutory power must be executed strictly for the purposes for which it is given, and all the requirements of the statute in regard to obtaining and exercising the authority must be strictly followed.2 §33. When Will Is Silent. Although not expressly authorized by the will, an executor may, under discretionary power to dispose of the property and settle an estate, make a valid mortgage and borrow money to pay the debts of the estate. Under a limited discretion concerning division of the property an executor cannot authorize a mortgage on an undivided interest of one of the heirs.

§ 34. Disability of Insanity. A mortgage made by one who was insane at intervals, both before and after the execution of it, as to its validity, depends upon the question whether he was sane at the time, and the fact of his sanity must in such case be established at the time of executing the mortgage. A test of insanity frequently employed in cases of this kind is the knowledge of the extent and value of the property of the person in question, and his ability to transact ordinary business. §38. Married Women. At common law, a married woman could not make a mortgage, even to secure the payment of the purchase money of real estate conveyed to her. In equity, however, she has long occupied quite a different position in regard to her own property, and her power to contract in relation to it. The doctrine in England, adopted also in some of our states, is that the separate property of a married woman is answerable for her debts and engagements to the full extent to which it is subject to her disposal. That is the rule in Michigan. A married woman can bind herself personally only by such obligations as have reference to her separate property. She is not generally bound, therefore, by a note given by her alone or jointly with her husband for a debt of the husband.12 The statute permitting her to mortgage her property mentioned below is an exception to the general rule. 

While in equity a mortgage made by a married woman may be valid as a lien upon her real estate, when the remedy has been exhausted against the mortgaged real estate, there is no further remedy against her unless the mortgage was made to secure money to be used for her individual estate, but a decree of foreclosure against husband and wife is conclusive as to the liability of the wife in proceedings for a deficiency.18 The power of a married woman to mortgage her property in the State of Michigan is covered by statutory enactment and decisions relative thereto.14

If a wife signs a mortgage and note merely as the wife of the mortgagor, to waive her right of dower, then she is not personally liable on an action on the note.14

§ 40. Mortgage by One Partner of His Interest. A 

mortgage made by a partner of his interest in partnership real estate, to one who knows it to be such, is not a mortgage of the partner's undivided interest in such real estate, but of his interest in the portion mortgaged after the payment of the firm debts upon a settlement of the partnership accounts.18 

§ 41. Land Purchased with Partnership Funds. Land conveyed to members of a copartnership as tenants in common, but purchased with copartnership funds and used for copartnership purposes, is treated in equity as copartnership personal property.19 

§ 42. Mortgage to Secure Partnership Debt. A valid mortgage of partnership property to secure a partnership debt may be made by one partner without express or implied assent of the other party.20

IV. CORPORATIONS. 

§ 43. Power to Mortgage. A corporation has the power to mortgage its real estate as an incident to the power to acquire and hold it and to make contracts in regard to it when the power is not expressly denied and is not inconsistent with the public obligations of the corporation.21 A general power to mortgage the whole of any property necessarily carried with it the power to mortgage a part of such property, provided the property is of such a nature as to be divisible without detriment to the corporate interest.22 

§ 44. Mortgage of Corporation De Facto. A mortgage by a corporation de facto is good until the state has interposed and declared its exercise of corporate powers a usurpation. Until this is done, it is assumed that the corporation de facto rightfully possessed and exercised corporate powers.23 

845. Religious Corporations. A religious corpora tion has in general under Michigan laws the same right to mortgage and create liens upon its property that any other corporation has. Such power may be conferred by statutes, by by-laws, articles of incorporation, or special resolution.24

 § 46. Powers of Stockholders and Directors. The power to mortgage resides in the body corporate, or, in other words, in the stockholders. The directors of a corporation without authority, either expressly or implied, derived from the stockholders, have no right to execute a mortgage or to authorize anyone to do so. In 

Michigan the board of directors of a corporation organized under the general corporation acts did not, prior to the passage of Act No. 327 P. A. '31, have power to mortgage the property of the corporation unless authorized so to do by holders of not less than two-thirds of the capital stock of the corporation, except as hereinafter mentioned, which consent was required to be given either in writing or by vote at a meeting of the stockholders called for that purpose upon the same notice as that required for the annual meeting of the corporation, and certificate under seal of the corporation that such consent was given by the stockholders in writing, or that it was given by vote at a meeting, as aforesaid, was required to be subscribed and acknowledged by the president or vice-president, and by the secretary or assistant-secretary of the corporation, and filed or recorded with the instrument. However, where the stockholders in the Articles of Association, or in an amendment thereto, conferred general authority upon the directors to mortgage the property of the corporation, such consent and such certificate was not required, but the mortgage should have contained reference to such authority.25

These provisions are applicable to mortgages given before the passage of the act above mentioned. But such act, section 10, subdivision D, gives to the corporation power to mortgage its real property, and subdivision K of the same section provides that the powers of a corporation, except as otherwise provided in said act, shall be exercised by the board of directors. There are no other specific provisions in the act with reference to this matter.

V. POWER TO MORTGAGE. 

§ 48. Must Be Generally Specific. A power to sell and convey real estate does not confer a power to mortgage, and a mortgage executed under a power of attorney authorizing the attorney to sell and convey only is void.97

A bank organized under the National Banking Act is authorized to take and hold a mortgage of real estate by way of security for debts previously contracted, but not to take such a mortgage as security for debts contracted at the time or for future advances. The Supreme 

Court has held that the prohibition in the National Banking Act of a loan made upon real estate security does not make such a loan void, but that such a mortgage is valid between the parties and may be enforced; that the remedy for the violation of the statute would be forfeiture of the bank's charter.28 

§ 49. To Secure Joint Debt. It was held in early

§ 53. 

Accessions to Mortgaged Property. At com mon law, nothing can be mortgaged that does not belong to the mortgagor at the time the mortgage is made, but a different rule prevails in equity. Equity will give effect to a mortgage embracing interest to be acquired in the future. A railroad company having power to borrow money and secure it by a mortgage on its property may mortgage property to be acquired subsequently. 

This doctrine has been held to apply to a de facto corporation. A mortgage of all the property of a railroad company, including its franchises, etc., contemplates property owned both at the time of the mortgage and that to be subsequently acquired." 

§ 54. Mortgage of Corporate Franchises. A mort gage conveying the corporate property and appurtenances, and also its corporate franchises, incumbers only the franchise necessary to make the conveyance productive and beneficial to the grantees-namely, the franchise to maintain, manage, and operate the corporation and receive the income and profits thereof for its own benefit, and not the franchise to be a corporation or the general corporate powers.5

§ 55. Agreement to Mortgage. An agreement to give a mortgage or security on certain property, not objectionable for want of consideration, is treated in equity as a mortgage, upon the principle that equity will treat that as done which by agreement is to be done." 

§ 56. Parol Agreements. Although a parol agreement in respect to lands while it remains altogether executory is not enforceable, yet, when there has been a part performance of it, it cannot in equity be avoided."

An instrument which does not transfer the legal estate may yet operate as an equitable transfer of it in the nature of a mortgage. 

§ 57. Mortgage Imperfectly Executed. An unsealed instrument pledging the real and personal estate of a corporation for the performance of a contract is an equitable mortgage.⁹

§ 61. In General. Sometimes the question is very important as to whether a transaction of this nature is construed as the making of a mortgage or of a deed constituting a conditional sale. It may be of advantage to the person making the deed that it should be considered as a conditional sale, as, if it is a mortgage, it must be to secure an indebtedness, and the indebtedness may not be entirely satisfied by a foreclosure of the mortgage.

Cases involving distinction between mortgages and conditional sales are usually brought before courts of equity for adjudication. Whether a conveyance be a mortgage or a conditional sale must be determined by consideration of all of the surrounding facts and circumstances of the case. If both parties to the instrument intend that it shall operate merely as a security for a debt, it is a mortgage, though in form of an absolute deed.¹ Usually in doubtful cases the court will 

1 Gogarn v. Connors, 188 Mich. 

161; Wasey v. Whitcomb, 167 Mich. 58. 30

ABSOLUTE DEED GIVEN AS MORTGAGE 

[§ 62 construe the contract to be a mortgage rather than a conditional sale. Where a contract is construed as a mortgage, it is indispensable that a debt by the grantor to the grantee should exist for which the conveyance is security. While a mortgage may be redeemed at any time before the right is cut off by foreclosure, there can be no redemption under a conditional sale after the day appointed. 

§ 62. Character of Transaction Fixed at Inception. 

The character of a transaction is fixed at its inception. 

This fact has given rise to the maxim, "Once a mortgage, always a mortgage." If it was a conditional sale at the start, no lapse of time will make a mortgage of the transaction. On the other hand, if it was a mortgage at the start, it will remain a mortgage, and the rights of the parties will be governed by the law in relation to mortgages. The rules of law and equity are the same with respect to the obligation of the security. In both cases the intention of the parties that the conveyance is to stand merely as a security for debt stamps it as a mortgage.

This rule has been held not to prevent parties by a subsequent agreement from changing the instrument into an absolute conveyance. It has been held that once a mortgage, always a mortgage" does not mean that the right of redemption cannot be lost excepting under foreclosure. Title may not be passed by estoppel, it is true, but when passed by warranty deed and the grantor claims parol right of defeasance he may, by agreement or acts evidencing such purpose or bringing such result, cancel the secret agreement and let the terms of the deed control.8 66 8b One has a right to deed away his property, and at the same time, make a reservation of the right to repurchase 58.

§ 62a. Amount Secured by the Instrument. It is diffi cult to discover any good reason for giving a deed instead of using a mortgage form when securing the payment of an indebtedness. Doubtless the custom arose under the idea that where a deed was given the mortgagee could take possession of the property without foreclosure in case of default. There are certain early cases which would seem to justify this conclusion. But under the law as it now exists, such a mortgage could only be foreclosed by a suit in chancery. One of the objections to the giving of a deed to secure an indebtedness is that disputes may arise as to the amount of such indebtedness where the same rests in parol. It has been held that where a deed given to a bank as a mortgage, and so recorded, recited consideration of $6,800, and the bank, on inquiry by prospective purchasers of mortgaged property, informed them that that was the amount of lien, and they, relying thereon, purchased property, the bank is estopped from thereafter claiming any greater amount by reason of recitals in renewal note, given by mortgagor after the purchase, that security should cover every other obligation of mortgagor due and to become due.

§ 63a. Burden of Proof. The natural and prima facie effect of a conveyance expressing no condition and regularly executed in the presence of attesting witnesses, and duly acknowledged as an absolute deed, ought not to be controlled and qualified by oral evidence, and brought down to the effect due to a mere security on a slight showing. The great current of authority is distinct in holding that the party thus seeking to modify the operation of the instrument and prove himself entitled against the terms of his own deed to an equity of redemption is not only bound to make out that the transaction was in truth and justice nothing more than the giving of security, but is required to do so by a force of evidence sufficient to command the unhesitating assent of every reasonable mind." In Gogarn v. § 71. Description of Obligation Not Necessary. It is not generally necessary that the amount of the debt be stated in the mortgage, whether the sum be certain or uncertain, but it is better conveyancing to state the amount of an ascertained debt.¹

OBLIGATION SECURED 

[§ 73 A mortgage may be given to secure the payment of a portion of an obligation.¹ª

When a mortgage is given to secure future advances, it is not practical to state in the mortgage itself anything more than the limitation to which such advances may reach.

A mortgage to secure all of the debts from the grantor to the grantee and all liabilities of the latter as surety for the former is valid without a more particular description. Under the law providing for a specific tax on mortgages and like securities it is necessary, except in certain instances specified therein that either by the mortgage itself or by a sworn statement made at the time of recording the instrument the amount of the lien claimed shall appear, and one taking a mortgage for future advances should see that the specific tax is paid upon the full amount for which he will claim a lien upon the mortgaged property.3

A mortgage given for a greater sum than the amount due, without fraudulent intent, is valid to the extent of the actual debt. In such case, the mortgagor may show that the lien was for a less sum than that expressed in the mortgage.* 

§ 72. Instrument Should Identify the Thing Secured. 

It is not necessary that all of the particular note or other obligation be set forth in the mortgage if the paper is sufficiently described to identify it. The possession and production of the paper at trial are prima facie evidence that it is the same mentioned in the mortgage."

874. Extension of Lien by Renewal. The renewal of the original note or mortgage does not affect the security, nor does an extension of the time of payment waive other terms and conditions of the mortgage except by initiating a new period for the statute of limitations.10 

§ 75. Attempt to Enlarge or Extend Lien. A mort gage for a specified sum cannot be enlarged or extended to cover other debts or further advances, as against others who have acquired rights in the property.¹¹ 

Neither can the mortgagor as against them increase the charge upon the land by confessing judgment and thus compounding the interest. A mortgage given to secure future advances, not to exceed a certain amount, is valid and is a lien on the mortgaged property for advances not exceeding the amount specified, but a mortgage reciting that it was given for a note and such future advances as may be made during a given year secures the note only.12 

§ 76. 

Taxes and Assessments. There is an apparent exception to the rule that the mortgage debt cannot, as against third persons, be increased after the execution of the mortgage, and that is, where money is paid by the mortgagee to redeem the premises from a tax sale or from any charge which is a paramount lien upon the property.18 §77. Solicitor's Fee. In addition to the mortgage debt, the mortgage may be made to secure the payment of a reasonable fee of a solicitor in case of a foreclosure of the mortgage. The laws of the states differ somewhat upon this proposition.14

 § 78. Increasing the Rate of Interest. The parties to a mortgage cannot, as against subsequent purchasers or incumbrancers, stipulate by an unrecorded agreement for a higher rate of interest than that provided by the mortgage as recorded. But a provision in the mortgage that in case either payments upon the principal or interest shall not be made when due, the same shall bear interest at a larger rate, will be enforced. While it is true that a limitation is necessary in order to constitute a continuing security which will not be affected by subsequent conveyances, a recorded mortgage for an unlimited sum is notice to a subsequent incumbrancer as to all sums advanced upon the mortgage before the subsequent lien attaches.15 If such mortgagee is not under any obligation to make advances, and after notice of a subsequent mortgage does make further advances, to the extent of such advances, the subsequent mortgagee has the right of precedence. But if such mortgagee is under obligation to make the advances, he is entitled to the security, whatever may be the incumbrances subsequently made upon the property, and whether he has notice of them or not.16

§ 80. Notice of Nature of Such Mortgage. A mort gage for the payment of such sums of money as the mortgagee might advance in pursuance of an agreement mentioned in the conditions of a certain bond given by the mortgagee to the mortgagor of even date, contains reasonable notice of the incumbrance.18

It is provided under the laws of the State of Michigan that a tax of fifty cents shall be imposed for each one hundred dollars and each remaining major fraction thereof of the principal debt or obligation which is or under any contingency may be secured by a mortgage upon real property situated within this state recorded on or after the first day of January, 1912.18 The same act provides for the payment of specific tax to the treasurer of the county wherein the property is situated and the filing of a certificate from him which is to be recorded by the Register of Deeds as a part of the record of the said mortgage. Thus, notice is given where future advances are to be made of the extent to which such advances are expected, and one examining such record has the right to rely thereon. It has been held that where a deed was given to a bank as a mortgage and so recorded, which recited a consideration of $6,800, and where the bank, on inquiry by prospective purchasers of mortgaged property, informed them that that was the amount of the lien, and where they examined the record and found that the specific tax had been paid as for a mortgage of $6,800, that the bank was thereafter estopped from claiming that a loan had been made for a larger amount of money under the terms of a note which provided for future advances.18b

III. MORTGAGE OF INDEMNITY. 

§ 81. Description of Indemnity. Very much of what has already been said in regard to present and future debts secured by mortgagee is applicable to mortgage made to indemnify a mortgagee against liability incurred by him in behalf of the mortgagor.

An indemnity mortgage is sufficient as such if the debt or obligation against which the mortgagee is intended to be protected is described with reasonable certainty.19 

§ 82. When It Becomes a Lien. A mortgage of in demnity to a surety is a lien from the time of its execution and delivery, and not merely from the time when the mortgagee pays the debt on which he is surety. Parol evidence is admissible to show the true character of a mortgage. Although it is given for a definite sum and secures the payment of notes for definite amounts, it may be shown that it is simply one of indemnity, or for future advances.20

I. INSURABLE INTEREST. 

§ 88. Nature of Fire Insurance. The only lawful pur pose of a contract of insurance is to indemnify some person having an interest in the subject matter of such insurance against loss. §89. Interest of Mortgagor. The mortgagor may insure the full value of property and recover for the full amount insured if, at the time of the loss, he had the right of redemption,' and it matters not that the mortgagee has taken possession of the premises. A mortgagee 

1 Royal Ins. Co. v. Stinson, 103 

U. S. 25, 26 L. Ed. 473. 53

90] 

and mortgagor may both insure their separate interests at the same time. Where the mortgagee and mortgagor insure their respective interests in property in different companies, each company is liable in case of loss according to the insurable interest of the insured in the property. The insurable interest of the holder of the mortgage is measured by the value of his lien, if this does not exceed the value of the property. 

The mortgagor's interest remains insurable so long as he has a right to redeem the land. It continues after a sale of his equity of redemption on execution until his right to redeem from such sale is barred; and he may recover the insurance notwithstanding the sale.³ 

§ 90. When Application Should State Incumbrance. 

The existence of a mortgage upon a building, for the insurance of which application is made, is a material fact if inquired about, and any misrepresentation in regard to the existence of the incumbrance or the amount of it will render the policy void.*

§ 92. When Covenant or Agreement to Insure. § 93. 

Who May Bring Suit. When the policy is taken out by the mortgagor in his name, payable in case of loss to the mortgagee, the mortgagor should, with the assent of the mortgagee, sue on the policy in his own name. 

This direction in the policy is not an assignment of it, and although it is assented to by the insurer, the contract with the mortgagor is not thereby merged or extinguished.

The rights of the mortgagee, and of the insurers as well, may be protected in all cases by payment of money into court.

There can be no division of causes of action on a single insurance policy. Whoever sues must be able to enforce the whole liability. I. WHAT FIXTURES ARE COVERED BY A MORTGAGE. 

§100. When Part of the Realty. A mortgage of real property, as a general rule, carries as part of the security, all fixtures belonging to the realty without any 59

§ 101] 

special mention of them being made in the conveyance. 

In determining what chattels annexed to the land become fixtures, and therefore bound by a mortgage, very much the same rules apply as between a grantor and his grantee in case of an absolute conveyance.¹ § 101. Intention. The intention with which an article of personal property is attached to the realty, whether for temporary use or for permanent improvement, has within certain limits quite as much to do with the determination of the question whether it has thereby become a permanent fixture, as has the way and the manner in which it is attached. § 102. General Rule. The criterion adopted by several courts for determining whether property ordinarily regarded as personal becomes a part of the realty is the united application of the following requisites: First, actual annexation to the realty, or something appurtenant thereto; second, appropriateness to the use or purpose of that part of the realty with which it is connected; third, the intention of the party making the annexation to make the article a permanent accession to the freehold-his intention being inferred from the nature of the article affixed, the relation and situation of the party making the annexation, the structure and mode of annexation, and the purpose or use for which the annexation has been made. 

§ 103. Treated as Separate Property. The fact that a chattel has been mortgaged before, or at the time it was attached to the realty, has weight as an implied agreement between the parties in leading to the deter-

§105. Agreement of Parties. The parties to a mort gage may by agreement at the time of the execution of a mortgage determine that certain articles upon the mortgaged land shall not be covered by the mortgage as fixtures, and the agreement will control, even if, as a matter of law, such articles would generally pass with the land as fixtures. In such case the fixture will be removable, notwithstanding the annexation was permanent in character, provided always that the removal can be made without any permanent material damage to the estate. 

§ 106. Chattels Attached After Mortgage Given. 

Chattels attached to the realty after the execution of a mortgage of it become a part of the mortgage security if they are attached for the permanent improvement of the estate and not for a temporary purpose and are adapted to the use to which the realty is devoted, if they are such as are regarded as permanent in their nature." 

The same rule applies to articles annexed to the premises by a subsequent grantee or vendee in possession under an executory contract to purchase.

II. MACHINERY IN MILLS. 

§ 112. Nature of Use. A distinction is properly made between such fixtures in a mill as are indispensable to its use as a mill, and the movable machines used in it, which may be dispensed with upon a change in business to which the mill may be readily adapted. Of the former class are such as are used for furnishing the motive power; and if the mill is adapted to one business only, the machinery necessary for that business may be included in the same class.14 

§ 113. Machinery Especially Adapted to the Purpose of Manufacturing Plant. To this class also belongs machinery especially adapted to carry out the purposes for which the plant was erected, and presumably to increase its value, although it may be removed without injury to the building.15 

§ 114. Movable Machines. Of the other class are mov able machines used in a mill adapted to various kinds of business, which may be wholly set aside and still the value and usefulness of the mill property would not be materially impaired. Such machinery, not being indispensable to the enjoyment of the realty, is generally considered not to be a part of it, and not to pass by a mortgage of it.16 23.

III. ROLLING STOCK OF RAILWAYS. 

§ 120. Decisions Conflicting. Whether the rolling stock and fixtures of a railroad are personal property, or are in some sense fixtures, and therefore pass by a mortgage of the realty, is a question that has been much discussed, and the decisions are conflicting. The federal courts have held that all property essential to the operation of a railroad, including the right of way, road bed, ties, rails, side tracks, switches, depots, station houses, water tanks, and other fixtures, together with the rolling stock and other necessary movable appliances are real estate.24

The extent of property covered by a railroad mortgage is a matter of interpretation under the rules applicable to the interpretation of mortgages by individuals, reference, however, being had to the authorizing statute.25 

Fixtures, whether acquired before or after the execution of such mortgage, are subject to its lien.26 

IV. REMEDIES FOR REMOVAL OF FIXTURES. 

§ 121. Rights of Mortgagee. The mortgagee may fol low and take fixtures covered by a mortgage of the realty, and improperly removed, wherever he can find them.

The mortgagor himself can of course gain no right to hold them as against the mortgagee. A purchaser from the mortgagor has no such right, because he is affected with knowledge of the existing lien, and, as against the

I. NATURE AND APPLICATION OF REGISTRY LAWS. 

§ 124. In General. In most of the states, mortgages are required by statute to be recorded in the same manner as other conveyances of real property, in order to charge third persons acquiring an interest in the property, such as subsequent purchasers, mortgagees, and judgment creditors. In general, the statutes provide that such conveyances shall not be valid as against persons other than the grantor, his heirs and devisees, and persons having notice thereof, unless they are recorded in the registry of deeds for the county in which the land is situated.¹

The order of priority between persons claiming liens on the same property, by mortgage or otherwise, is fixed by the order in which they are filed for record. 

In most states all instruments relating to the title of real estate are recorded in the same books of record. In some states, however, it is provided by statute that all mortgages shall be recorded in separate books kept for this purpose only. § 125. Deed Absolute in Form. A deed absolute in form intended as a mortgage should be recorded in the book of mortgages, and has been held void as to subse-

Assignee of Bankrupt. Equitable mortgages are generally held to be within the recording acts as much as are legal mortgages.16 At first a different interpretation was put upon the acts, and a mortgage of an equity or of an equitable estate was not constructive notice when registered. But at an early day in this country it was established, either judicially or by statute that all rights, incumbrances or conveyances touching or in any way concerning land, should appear upon the public records, and that conveyances of equitable interests as well as legal were within the registry acts. A mortgage, therefore, of such an interest if first recorded is preferred to a mortgage of the legal estate. 

Generally the record of an agreement constituting an equitable mortgage is notice to a subsequent purchaser of the legal estate from the same grantor.17 One in possession of lands under a parol contract to purchase them may mortgage his interest in them, and the record of the mortgage will be notice to subsequent purchasers and incumbrancers.18

§ 139. Assignees of Mortgages. The registration laws and the doctrines of priority by record generally extend to assignments of mortgages as well, either by express provisions of statute or by judicial construction.20 And an assignment is invalid against subsequent purchasers without notice unless it is recorded. Consequently, if a mortgagee transfers the note secured by the mortgage, or makes a formal assignment of the mortgage which is not recorded, and afterward enters a satisfaction of the mortgage upon the record, or if the mortgagee takes a conveyance of the equity of redemption, and then with an apparent ample title conveys the property to another, the mortgage ceases to be a lien as against one who purchases the property in good faith and without notice.21

§ 140. Mortgage Securing Negotiable Paper. A mort gage securing negotiable paper is a mere incident thereto and partakes in its negotiability. The law of negotiable instruments governs the rights of parties thereto as well as third parties concerning payment; and payment before maturity to anyone other than the holder of the negotiable instrument is at the risk of the payer, and is binding upon the holder of the paper only where express or implied authority to receive such payment existed. Consequently payment of a negotiable note secured by a mortgage, by the mortgagor or his grantee, when made to the mortgagee not in possession of the note and mortgage, is not binding upon an assignee thereof before maturity, who has possession of the papers at the time of payment unless he had expressly or impliedly authorized such payment.24

If there is a formal and valid assignment of a mortgage and the debt secured by it, the assignee is invested with all the rights, powers and equities of the mortgagee.25

It is sometimes provided by statute that a deed shall be deemed to be recorded when it is filed for record, or noted in an entry book by the recorder as received. IV. ERRORS IN THE RECORD. 

§ 154. Defective Record. If the record of a deed be defective for any cause, it is constructive notice of only what the record contains, in case the record is not an accurate transcript of the instrument. Persons interested in a title have a right to resort to the records to find out the contents of a deed, and can be considered as having notice of it only as it appears of record. Every requirement of statute in relation to the execution and acknowledgment or proof of a deed or mortgage must be complied with in order to gain priority by the record of it.48 However, a reasonable and practical compliance with the statute is all that is necessary. Where the rule is that the deed is operative as a record from the time it is filed for record, the apparent weight of authority is that any error in transcribing the deed, as for instance in the date, does not prejudice the grantee or mortgagee.**

V. EFFECT OF RECORD DULY MADE. 

§ 157. Constructive Notice. The record of a deed or mortgage is constructive notice to all subsequent purchasers and mortgagees in the line of title. This constructive notice, while preventing any claim on the part of the purchaser against the mortgagee, does not prevent the purchaser from maintaining an action against the grantor for false representations.47 Subsequent purchasers are entitled to rely upon the record and are not charged with notice of latent equities or facts not disclosed or suggested by the record itself.48 

§ 158. Unrecorded Mortgage. Where one purchases land in good faith without notice of an unrecorded mortgage he takes it discharged of the lien, and he can convey a good title to it, although the mortgage is recorded before he conveys and his vendee has notice of it.49 

After the mortgage is made and recorded, the record of any deeds subsequently made by the mortgagor is not notice to the mortgagee but other facts and circumstances may be sufficient to put him on his guard so that he should examine the record before releasing parts of the premises from the mortgage.50

 § 159. Extent of Notice. The record of the mortgage is notice of an incumbrance for the amount specified in it, or so referred to as to put subsequent purchasers upon inquiry as to the extent of the lien. If it specifies the amount secured, it is notice only to the extent and amount of the debt stated and cannot be enlarged to include any other debts and claims not specified or referred to."¹ 

§ 160. Purchase Money Mortgage. If a purchaser of land, at the instant of receiving his deed, executes and delivers two mortgages of it, one to his grantor to secure a payment of a part of the purchase money and the other to a third person and all the instruments are entered for record at the same moment, the mortgage to his grantor takes precedence. The deed and mortgage for purchase money are parts of one transaction and give the purchaser only an instantaneous seizin.52

It has been held that where purchase money mortgage on city lots provided that it should be subsequent to mortgage or mortgages thereafter placed on premises not exceeding 50 per cent of total cost of lot and buildings, no covenant could be implied postponing effect of such clause until buildings should be erected thereon, notwithstanding claim that its sole purpose was to enable purchaser to obtain mortgages on lots on which buildings should be erected.52a 

§ 161. Torrens System. A system of recording instru ments in the United States which has caused much litigation is the Torrens system. I. IN GENERAL. 

§ 162. Subsequent Purchasers with Notice. The doc trine of notice as affecting priority is generally adopted in this country. Subsequent purchasers, who have notice of a prior unrecorded mortgage are affected by their knowledge of it in the same way that the prior record of the mortgage would affect them. A mortgagee who has actual knowledge or legal notice of a prior conveyance, mortgage, or other lien on the premises, takes subject thereto, and is not protected as a bona fide purchaser. Thus a subsequent mortgagee who has actual 86

NOTICE AS AFFECTING PRIORITY 

[§ 165 or constructive notice of a prior mortgage will take subject to it.¹

II. ACTUAL NOTICE. 

§ 163. What Is Notice. There are three kinds of notice: Actual, implied, and constructive. Since the doctrine of notice as affecting the priority of incumbrances arises from the equitable view that it is fraud in one, who has notice of an adverse claim in another, to attempt to acquire a title to the prejudice of the interest of which he has been made aware, it is obvious that the actual culpability involved by the notice must depend altogether upon the kind and degree of notice received. 

Yet the legal consequences are the same provided the notice is imputed at all. Actual notice literally means direct personal knowledge." § 164. Definition. Actual notice is such as will give direct personal knowledge and one who has such knowledge of a fact is said to have actual notice thereof. 

Actual notice is not limited to express knowledge directly communicated. It includes knowledge of facts and circumstances so pertinent in character as to enable reasonably cautious and prudent persons to investigate and ascertain the ultimate facts. Whether actual knowledge exists in any particular case and whether knowledge which one possesses with reference to a fact is sufficient to charge him with notice is a question of fact to be considered and determined upon the evidence in each particular case.

III. IMPLIED NOTICE. 

§ 165. Circumstances Raising Implication. Notice may be implied from circumstances that will give rise to the implication that the party surrounded by such

Actual notice under this constructive form includes all instances of actual notice established by circumstantial evidence. If a party has knowledge of such facts as would lead a fair and prudent man using ordinary caution to make further inquiries, and he avoids the inquiry he is chargeable with the notice of facts which by ordinary diligence he would have ascertained. 

He has no right to shut his eyes against the light before him and he does a wrong who does not heed the signs and signals seen by him. It may be well concluded that he is avoiding notice of that which he in reality believes or knows and which to the mind of a prudent man would amount to notice. Means of knowledge with a duty of using them are in equity equivalent to knowledge itself. § 166. Sources of Information. The degrees and kinds of notice from which it may be held that actual notice is implied runs from a firm written statement of facts sufficient to put a person upon his inquiry to mere verbal declarations of such facts. It may be given expressly as a notice, or it may have come in an accidental way, but neither the form nor purpose of the notice is material; a verbal communication may be sufficient. Flying reports may not be considered as bringing notice. As has frequently been said flying reports are many times fables and not truths. The information must be sufficient to furnish a basis of opinion and mere rumor and suspicion that some other person claims an interest in the property will not affect a person with notice of such interest.5

§ 168. Purchaser with Notice from One Without No tice. A purchaser with notice may acquire a good title from one who was a purchaser for value without notice. 

The rule that a purchaser of property, with notice of some prior adverse claim to, or interest in, such property, takes subject to such interest, is subject to the limitation that, if a person with such notice acquires a legal title to the property from one who is without such notice, he is entitled to the same protection as his vendor, as otherwise it would mar the value of the one who acquired the property without notice as it would limit the persons to whom he would be subject to sell a title which is regarded as valid in him. But the title of a purchaser without notice cannot be transferred free from equities back to a prior grantor who was charged with notice at the time he acquired his former title, for a purchaser cannot be allowed to clear off the existing equities of which he had notice, by transferring the title to an innocent purchaser, and then repurchasing the property. 8a

§ 172. Priority as Between Unrecorded Mortgages. 

As between several unrecorded mortgages or other conveyances those having priority of execution take precedence.18

In determining such priority fractions of a day will usually be considered. Successive mortgages upon the same property are entitled to priority of payment out of its proceeds in the order in which they have attached as liens upon it; however, under exceptional circumstances where there are special equities a junior lien may be given a preference.

In a suit to foreclose a mortgage, a second mortgage given to raise funds to complete a building on the premises, which was recorded before the first mortgage, of which the second mortgagee had no notice, it has been held that the second mortgagee was entitled to priority to the extent of the actual consideration therefor.12a

I. IN GENERAL. 

§ 175. Lex Rei Sitae. The validity of a mortgage is usually a subject to be determined by the lex rei sitae. 

Thus, the question whether a mortgagor is competent to give a mortgage must usually be decided by that law, for on his competency depends the validity of the mortgage with respect to sufficiency of parties.¹ However, it is to be observed that as mortgages are generally in the nature of collateral security for a personal obligation, the validity of the mortgage tested by the lex rei sitae may be of no avail, for the reason that the obligation which it secures tested by its proper law, the lex loci contractus, may be invalid, a circumstance that would, of course, vitiate the mortgage. Thus, a mortgage secured by a married woman in one jurisdiction on property located in another has been held invalid, although she was competent under the lex rei sitae to make a mortgage, because under the lex loci contractus she was incapable of contracting the personal obligation which the mortgage was given to secure. 

157 L. R. A. 820n. 

2 Burr v. Beckler, 264 Ill. 230, 106 N. E. 206, L. R. A. 1916 A 

1049, Ann. Cas. 1915 D 1132; Palmer v. Mason, 42 Mich. 146. 94

VALIDITY OF INSTRUMENTS 

[§ 176 § 176. General Rule. A mortgage is governed by the same rules of construction and interpretation that apply to written instruments generally, and particularly to deeds. The intention of the parties is to be sought not only from the form of the instruments, but also from the situation of the parties and the nature and object of their transactions. The printed part of a mortgage is as much a part of the instrument and as strongly binds the parties thereto as the written part though if there is a conflict between the two the written part will prevail. 

A mortgage and a note secured by it are to be deemed parts of one transaction and are construed together as such; both should be given effect if possible. The intention of the parties as determined from the examination of both, not from one separately, must prevail. Where there is a difference between the terms of bonds and of the mortgage given to secure them as to the payment of interest the terms of the bonds will control. (See supra, Section 17). 

The law in force at the time a mortgage is executed is the law which determines the force and effect of the mortgage, so a mortgage of lands lying at the time in one jurisdiction, but subsequently becoming a part of another would ordinarily be construed according to the laws of the jurisdiction wherein lay the lands when the mortgage was executed, but the rights of a purchaser under such a mortgage are to be determined as of the time he obtained deed, that being the time when his rights attached.

It is difficult to formulate a rule by which questions concerning the construction of mortgages may be referred, either to the jurisdiction wherein the property mortgaged is situated, or to the law of some other jurisdiction. It may be said in general that those relating distinctly and directly to the mortgage as distinguished from the personal obligation only indirectly affecting the mortgage may be governed by another law. Under this principle the sufficiency of the execution of a mortgage is governed by lex rei sitae irrespective of the place 95

§ 177] 

wherein the mortgage was executed, the debt secured by it contracted or made payable.

In Michigan one cannot introduce a mortgage in evidence without having paid the specific tax thereon.

§ 177. Valuable Consideration. It need not be one moving directly from the mortgagee to the mortgagor; but any benefit to the mortgagor or to a stranger, or damage or loss to the mortgagee, rendered or sustained at the request of the mortgagor, is sufficient. A liability to loss on the part of the mortgagee is consideration for a mortgage given to secure him against it, as much as is a direct benefit to the mortgagor, of whatever nature it may be. The real consideration may always be shown if it becomes material.*

§ 179. Mortgage Under Seal. A mortgage under seal implies consideration at common law, and none need be proved, and it is good if it is shown that none was given.

§ 181. Illegality of Consideration. Illegality of con sideration invalidates a mortgage, whether it consists in a violation of the common law or of a statute." 

Knowledge on the part of the mortgagee that the mortgage money is to be used for an illegal purpose is no defense to foreclosure proceedings.

A mortgage given to secure a debt made illegal by statute, as for instance, a debt incurred for intoxicating liquors illegally sold to the mortgagor cannot be enforced; and such a mortgage is invalid although not given to the seller of the liquors, but at his request to a creditor of his, who knew that the consideration was illegal.

I. IN GENERAL. 

§ 182. What Law Governs. There is some authority for the position that the lex rei sitae necessarily controls when the question is presented whether the obligation secured by a mortgage is affected with usury, irrespective of the place where the contract was made, or where the debt is payable, or of the intention of the parties as to what law should govern. However, the great weight of authority is opposed to this view, and holds that a mortgage on real property is to be tested by the same law with respect to usury that applied to the personal obligation, which it secures, and not generally by the lex rei sitae.¹ A mortgage valid where executed and according to the lex rei sitae is not invalidated, it has been held, because usurious by the law of the jurisdiction wherein the mortgagee resides and the debt is payable. 

§ 183. Enforcement of Lien. The lex rei sitae gov erns as to proceedings to foreclose a mortgage, the manner and terms of sale thereunder, the terms of redemption of the land from the sale, and similar matters. 

A loan by a corporation domiciled in one state, to a citizen of another state, and secured by a mortgage on land in the latter state, has been governed in the settlement of interest on foreclosure by the law of such latter state, although the contract of loan and mortgage stipulates that it is solvable by the laws of the state of the domicile of the corporation, and is made with reference to its laws.2 

§ 184. Effect of Usury. Usury laws apply to mort gages in the same manner that they apply to contracts in general, the same principles of law are applicable when questions arise as to whether mortgages are usuri- 

1 Burr v. Beckler, 264 Ill. 230, 160 N. E. 206, L. R. A. 1916 A 

1048; Palmer v. Mason, 42 Mich. 146. 

2 National Mut. Building & Loan 

Ass'n v. Burch, 124 Mich. 57. 99

§ 185] 

ous or not, only in a few states at the present time will usury invalidate a contract. In Michigan the legal rate of interest is five per cent, but parties may contract in writing for not exceeding seven per cent. Usury will not cause a forfeiture of a contract but it will cause the forfeiture of the right to recover any interest. A purchaser in good faith is not affected by the fact that negotiable instruments carry usurious interest providing that fact is not apparent upon the face of the instrument. 

The defense of usury is a personal matter and may be waived. 3a 

§ 185. National Banking Act. The National Banking 

Act provides that banks organized under it may take interest at the rate allowed by the laws of the state where the banks are located, and no more, except that where, by such laws a different rate is limited for banks of issue organized under state laws, the same rate shall be allowed the national banks. When no rate is fixed by state or territorial laws, national banks may take not exceeding seven per cent. The penalty for taking a greater rate of interest is a forfeiture of the entire interest reserved; and in case a greater interest has been paid, the debtor may recover twice the amount of the interest thus paid. This statute is exclusive of state legislation for taking usury.3b 

A debt cannot be avoided by reason of usury charged by a national bank; nor can a bank, by offering to remit the excess, evade the statute as to forfeiture of the entire interest.⭑

§ 186. Reasonableness of Agreement. The fact that there was included in the loan a commission to the lender for storing, weighing, and selling cotton belonging to

Where a borrower executes a mortgage negotiated by his broker in which, in compliance with the conditions imposed by the lender, the brokers' commissions are included, and the lender accepts the security and makes the loan, the broker does not thereby become the agent of the lender, and the loan is not rendered usurious by the commissions included in the mortgage.5 

Where a lumber company charged more for lumber sold on credit, for which a mortgage was given to it, than it would have charged had payment been made in cash, that fact would not render the mortgage usurious, under C. L. '15 (5998), C. L. '29 (9240).5a

Where a written contract provided that the owner of lots should deed them as security to a finance company, which would erect a building thereon, and then resell to the owner on a contract at a certain price, crediting thereon the agreed value of the lots, the transaction was a loan rather than a purchase and sale, and, therefore, the statute against usury is applicable thereto.5b

III. WHEN A BONUS IS PAID TO LOAN AGENT. 

§187. Agreement of Lender. It has been held that a loan is not rendered usurious by the fact that the agent of the lender, without the knowledge or consent of the latter, exacts from the borrower a bonus for his service in addition to the highest legal rate of interest, which the contract reserves for the benefit of the lender. 

But a charge of twenty per cent of the loan as commission made against the borrower by the lenders' agent, knowledge of which is imputed to the lender, makes the transaction usurious, where such commission and the interest added exceed the lawful rate of interest.

§ 188. 

Commissions or Bonuses. While there is some conflict of authority it may be said as a safe general rule that when a loan agent intervenes between the loaner and the borrower and charges a commission which added to the interest charged would make the rate exceed the legal rate for the period of the loan, if such agent was the agent for the borrower the contract would not be usurious; if he was the agent for the loaner such contract would be usurious.

VI. EXCHANGE AND PREMIUMS. 

§ 192. Place of Payment. It is usual to require the mortgage and interest thereon to be paid at the home or office of the mortgagee. If these are made payable at the place of residence of the mortgagor for his accommodations it is not usurious for him to allow the mortgagee the difference of exchange between the two places; unless it appear this allowance was a mere device on the part of the mortgagee to evade the usury laws, and to obtain more than a legal interest for the use of his money.14

VII. MORTGAGE TO BUILDING AND LOAN ASSOCIATION. 

§ 194. Fines and Impositions. It has been generally held that a mortgage to a building and loan association is not usurious when, under the articles of association, in addition to monthly payments of interest, the mortgagor is bound, both by the mortgage and as a member of the association, to pay certain fines and impositions. There are special provisions usually in the usury laws of the different states with reference to building and loan associations, and it has been generally held that the relation between the associations and the borrowing member consists of two separate contracts-the contract of membership and the contract of loan. In applying this view they hold that stock debts are not to be considered as paid upon the loan, and are not to be added in determining whether a usurious rate of interest has been charged.17

IX. EVIDENCE-BURDEN OF PROOF-PRACTICE. 

§ 196. Burden Upon the Mortgagor. The burden of proof that the mortgage is usurious is usually upon the mortgagor. He is attempting to impeach his own obligation and he must establish facts to constitute usury by a clear preponderance of the evidence. It has even been held in some cases that it must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt.20

The wrongful act of usury will never be imputed to the parties, and it will not be inferred when the opposite conclusion can be reasonably and fairly reached.21

§197. Rights of Mortgagor. A distinction is made between the rights of a mortgagor when defending on the ground of usury and his rights when he applies to a court of equity for relief against a usurious contract; for while in the former case he may avail himself fully of the statute, in the latter case he must do equity before he can obtain equity and must offer to pay the debt with legal interest.22 The Leach case, cited below, is of peculiar interest, not only because of the matter above mentioned to which it refers, but because of an interesting question in relation to pleadings. Leach filed a bill to redeem from an alleged usurious mortgage, to foreclose which defendant filed a cross-bill, and it was held that the trial court was not in error in declining to permit the defendant to so amend his answer as to eliminate the portion claiming affirmative relief, leaving the answer a mere denial of the averments of the bill, where it appeared that the result would prejudice complainant by reason of the fact that the amendment would leave the mortgagee in position to claim the legal interest, whereas, in the absence of such amendment, complainant would be relieved from the payment of interest. It has been held that the point made by defendant that the answer and cross-bill contained no prayer or request for usurious interest was immaterial in a suit to redeem from a mortgage; if it is sought to enforce by affirmative relief a contract tainted with usury the statute 23 becomes operative and the interest is forfeited.

Pleadings. Usury must be specially and particularly pleaded, or it will not be considered as a defense. X. VALIDITY OF AGREEMENT TO PAY COMPOUND INTEREST. 

$200. Compound Interest. It has been held that an executory contract for the payment of compound interest, where the total amount of interest to be paid would exceed simple interest at the maximum rate permitted by law, could not be enforced, but that the payment of such interest by the debtor understandingly does not constitute usury. The subject of usury has been discussed perhaps as much by the courts as any matter connected with securities, or the loaning of money, and sometimes the decisions seem to follow more questions of policy than strict analogy to legal principles. If one promises to give to another for the use of money the maximum amount of interest permitted by law, and at the date for the payment of interest should, instead of paying such interest, give his promissory note therefor, bearing interest at the maximum amount permitted by law, no one could complain of the illegality of such a transaction; indeed it might result in a great favor to the borrower. 

The borrower always has it within his power, where a contract is made for compounding interest, to pay the interest when the same shall fall due and prevent such compounding so that the compounding of interest would not necessarily result in a hardship to the borrower, and unless the borrower was delinquent in his interest would not result in usury at all. 

28 Vilas v. McBride, 62 Hun (N. 

Y.) 324. 

29 Malone v. Danforth, 137 Mich. 227. 109

§ 201] 

A distinction is made between compounding of interest, in which case interest is charged upon interest due at each rest period, and the charging of simple interest from the date when each payment of interest shall fall due under the contract until the date of payment. The latter method has usually been held valid.80 §201. Taking Interest in Advance. It has been held that taking interest in advance to the full amount permitted by law for the ordinary period of commercial paper is not usurious, although the result would be the same as to charge interest upon the interest for the period for which interest was collected in advance. This rule has been even extended so as to sanction the taking of interest in advance for a period of six months or a year.31

But it has been held that a reservation of interest in advance on a loan for five years is usurious, where the amount reserved and the amount contracted to be paid aggregate a sum in excess of the highest legal rate for the term of the loan.82 

§ 202. Computation of Interest. The rule for comput ing interest upon the making of partial payments is to apply the payment in the first place to the interest then due. This rule which has been called the Massachusetts or the United States rule, was laid down by Chancellor 

Kent as follows: "When partial payments have been made, apply the payment, in the first place, to the discharging of the interest then due. If the payment exceeds the interest, the surplus goes toward discharging the principal, and the subsequent interest is to be computed on the balance of the principal remaining due. If the payment be less than the interest, the surplus of interest must not be taken to augment the principal, but 80 Gay v. 

Berkey, 137 Mich. 658.

550, 24 N. E. 573.

[§ 202b the interest continues on the former principal until the period when the payments, taken together, exceed the interest due, and then the surplus is to be applied toward discharging the principal, and interest is to be computed on the balance as aforesaid."

This is the rule generally adopted in this country.38 

What is known as the Connecticut rule is to reckon upon the principal up to the liquidation of the indebtedness, and then the interest on payments up to the same time, and to deduct this latter amount from the principal and interest.

I. MANNER OF TRANSFERRING. 

§ 203. Law Governing. In Michigan a mortgagee, until foreclosure, has no interest in the premises mortgaged, even after condition broken, that he can convey unless at the same time he transfers the debt secured by the mortgage, and a conveyance undertaken by him cannot operate as an assignment of the mortgage unless the intention that it should so operate by transferring the obligation secured is made clearly to appear.¹ 

§ 204. General Method of Assignment. Though a mortgage when given to secure a negotiable instrument partakes to some extent of the character thereof, it ordinarily has not of itself the qualities of negotiability. 

113 L. R. A. 295. 113

§ 205] 

However, when a note recites that it is secured by a mortgage it is none the less negotiable.1 The mortgage, however, is always assignable, without the concurrence or consent of, or notice to, the mortgagor, to anyone to whom the mortgagee pleases.

No particular form is essential to the assignment of a mortgage when made in conjunction with an assignment of the debt secured. The assignment must contain the name of an assignee and must identify the mortgage assigned, though for this latter purpose a description which gives the names of the mortgagor and mortgagee and the book and pages of the record where the mortgage is recorded is sufficient.

A quitclaim deed may be construed as an assignment of a mortgage.³ 

§ 205. Partial Assignment. A mortgage being in effect a lien to secure an obligation, the rule usually obtains that an assignment of the obligation, without an accompanying writing, operates as an assignment of the mortgage.¹

This is true, too, with respect to a deed of trust in nature of a mortgage and with respect to an equitable mortgage. It has frequently been held that the transfer of a bond or note passes to the transferee a mortgage given as security therefor, and this rule has been applied even where the transferee did not know of the existence of the mortgage at the time he purchased the note. In like manner bonds and notes secured by a mortgage are a proper subject of a gift causa mortis, without indorsement, and the mortgage will be carried with or without formal delivery. An assignment of a mortgage by transfer of the debt secured is generally as effectual for all purposes as a formal written assignment. It vests in the assignee a power of sale contained in the mortgage or a la Wilson v. Campbell, 110 Mich. 

580; Cox v. Cayan, 117 Mich. 599. 

2 Ladue v. Detroit & M. R. Co., 13 Mich. 380. 

3 Bradway v. Miller, 200 Mich. 648. 

4 Ladue v. Detroit & M. R. Co., 

13 Mich. 380. 114

TRANSFER OF INTEREST OF MORTGAGEE [§ 206 

statutory power implied therefrom. The assignee may exercise the right reserved to the mortgagee to declare the whole debt due on default in the payment of interest, and this is true though the mortgage does not purport to run in favor of, or to reserve powers in favor of, successors in interest of the mortgagee. But where the deed is regarded as necessary to complete the assignment, the transfer of the debt secured operates generally to vest in the assignee only an equitable interest in the mortgage, leaving the legal title with the mortgagee in trust. The assignment of part of the debt secured by a mortgage carries with it a proportional interest in the mortgage, though the courts are not in accord as to the rule by which the proceeds from the property should be distributed among various holders of parts of the indebtedness.5 

§ 206. Conflict Between Assignees. Where the holder of a mortgage indorses the note secured thereby before maturity, and later assigns the mortgage to a third person, fraudulently substituting another note for the one described in the mortgage, the first indorsee is entitled in equity to an assignment of the mortgage from such third person, though the situation of the parties is reversed if the note in fact secured is not indorsed but is assigned without indorsement. Where a mortgage is taken to secure the payment of negotiable promissory notes, and is then assigned and the assignment placed on record, all persons are chargeable with constructive notice of such assignment. This rule is the same though the notes were left in the possession of the original mortgagee and he sold and indorsed them to a purchaser in good faith and without actual notice of the prior assignment.Ⓡ

§ 207]  II. EFFECT OF TRANSFER. 

§ 207. Rights of the Assignee. When a valid and sufficient assignment has been made the assignee is invested with the powers and interests of the mortgagee as fully as if he had been named such in the mortgage. 

He may bring ejectment against the mortgagor or his lessee in jurisdictions wherein the mortgagee is entitled to possession, and if he enters he is fixed with the rights and duties of a mortgagee in possession. He may execute a power of sale granted in the mortgage whether the assignment was for collateral security or absolute." 

Even though an assignee gives for the mortgage less than its actual value he will nevertheless as a general rule be entitled to claim payment in full of the moneys secured by the mortgage unless he stands in a fiduciary position to the mortgagor, in which case recovery can be had only for the amount actually paid.³ 

The assignee of a mortgage takes the same subject to all equities existing against it in the hands of the assignor. Thus, the defense of prior payment may be pleaded against an assignee though a mortgage paid before maturity will be valid in the hands of a subsequent assignee for value who takes it without notice of the payment. The payment of a mortgage by an agent for and with the funds of the mortgagor discharges the mortgage, although the agent, instead of having it discharged, causes it to be assigned to secure a debt owing by himself. In such a case, neither the assignee nor one who takes an assignment from him can hold the mortgage as against the mortgagor or his heirs. So, usurious interest paid to a mortgagee may be pleaded as a counterclaim against the assignee of the mortgage.10 

An assignee of a trust mortgage which never took effect was held not to be entitled to the security even though the assignee advanced money to make a loan of

The mortgagor may be equitably estopped by his acts or otherwise from asserting a particular defense or defenses against the assignee or even the invalidity of the mortgage. Thus, where a mortgage is given, without consideration, to defraud creditors, it has been held that the dishonest mortgagor is equitably estopped from claiming that there was no consideration for the mortgage, as against a purchaser in good faith, for value, and without notice, and a mortgage delivered to a third person, without consideration, in order that he may procure money thereon for the mortgagor, and by him assigned for value is valid in the hands of the assignee for the money paid therefor by him even though the assignor fails to pay over the money to the mortgagor. So it has been decided that the assignee of a mortgage bona fide and without notice, takes it discharged of any secret trust with which the property may be bound in the hands of the mortgagor in favor of the mortgagee. The burden of establishing circumstances of estoppel rests upon the assignee.11 

§ 209. Equities Against Mortgagor. The interest of an assignee of a mortgage is not affected with equities against the assignor in favor of third persons of which the assignee had no notice, for although it is the duty of the assignee to inquire of the mortgagor, he is not required to inquire of the whole world as to latent equities.

It must be kept in mind that the failure to record an assignment does not obliterate the record of the mortgage, and so long as the mortgage remains unsatisfied a purchaser or subsequent incumbrancer of the property cannot be deemed to take without notice thereof, and his title or lien is therefore subject to that of the assignee. 

§ 217. Effect of Record. In general, the record of an assignment of a mortgage in compliance with the recording laws is notice to all the world, with the exception, in some jurisdictions, of the mortgagor.20

Accordingly it protects the assignee against any subsequent acts of the mortgagee affecting the mortgage, such as a subsequent assignment of the mortgage or a subsequent and unauthorized discharge or release of the mortgage, so the recording of the assignment by the assignee in the manner prescribed protects him from being bound by an instrument extending the time of the payment, which though executed before the assignment was not recorded previously.
