I. NATURE OF THE RIGHT OF SUBROGATION. 

§308. In General. Subrogation arises by operation of law whenever the mortgage debt has been extinguished by one other than the debtor who is entitled to redeem.¹ 

An assignment implies a continued existence of the debt, and the equitable right does not then arise. 

The doctrine of subrogation is resorted to for the purpose of doing justice between the parties. It will not be enforced to defeat or interfere with superior or equal equities of others, or with legal rights of others growing out of express contracts, or against one having both the legal and equitable title. The subrogation or substitution, by operation of law, arises or proceeds on the theory that the mortgage debt is paid. If the holder of a bond and mortgage assign them to a party claiming a right 

1 Jones on Mortgages, 8th Ed.,

Vol. 1, p. 976. 189

§ 309] 

1 to redeem, the latter is subrogated, by the assignment, to the mortgage debt and mortgage security, and to the instruments evidencing such debt and security and there is no room or occasion for subrogation by operation of law.

The doctrine sometimes spoken of as "legal subrogation," which has long been applied by courts of equity, rests upon the equitable principle that one who, in order to protect a security held by him, is compelled to pay a debt for which another is primarily liable, is entitled to be substituted in the place of, and to be vested with the rights of, the person to whom such payment is made, without agreement to that effect. "Conventional subrogation" arises from an agreement between a debtor and a third person whereby the latter, in consideration that the security of the creditor and all his rights thereunder be vested in him, agrees to make payment of the debt in order to relieve the debtor from a sacrifice of his property due to an enforced sale thereof, and while such right is wholly independent of any interest in the property which the lender may have to protect, it does not inure to a mere volunteer who has no equities which appeal to the conscience of the court. 

A mortgagee seeking the aid of a court of equity in the collection of a debt secured by a mortgage, may be required by said court, to prevent loss of the property by the mortgagor, to assign said mortgage to a third person, who, at the request of the mortgagor is ready and willing to advance the money to reimburse the first mortgagee for the money loaned, and interest accrued thereon, and all costs there incurred.1ª § 309. Equitable Principle. Under the equitable principle of subrogation, one who pays a mortgage debt under an agreement for an assignment or for a new mortgage, for his protection or for the benefit of another la French v. Grand Beach Co., 

239 Mich. 575. See also Walker v. 

Bates, 244 Mich. 582. 190

SUBROGATION 

[§ 312 acquires a right to the security held by the other, and upon the same ground a principal creditor succeeds to the security held by a surety whose liability has become fixed. If a mortgage on partnership real estate be discharged by one partner, when as between them it was the duty of the other to pay it, an equity arises in favor of the partner so paying the mortgage entitling him to indemnity through it." $310. Equitable Assignee. A purchaser at a foreclosure sale, supposing that he had obtained a good title by his purchase, sold the land to another by warranty deed. The mortgagor having recovered the land on account of irregularities in the foreclosure sale, the purchaser was sued upon his covenant of warranty in his deed of the property, and was obliged to pay the value of it; but he was subrogated to the rights of the mortgagee, as an equitable assignee. 

Such purchaser is regarded as the equitable assignee of the mortgage. And this right exists also in favor of a grantee or assignee of such purchaser.* 

§ 311. Subrogation of Stranger to Interest of Mort gagee. A stranger may be subrogated to the interest of a mortgagee, as against a subsequent mortgagee or purchaser, by force of an agreement made with the mortgagor at the time of paying the mortgage debt or any part of it to the mortgagee. This may be called a conventional subrogation, as mentioned above.

II. TEST OF RIGHT AND ILLUSTRATIONS. 

§ 314. Test of the Right of Subrogation. The test of the right of subrogation is found in answer to the inquiry whether the person who paid the mortgage debt is the one whose duty it was to pay it first of all; if the debt was not primarily his, and he only occupied the position of a surety to the mortgagor, he is entitled to be subrogated to the position of the mortgagee when he has paid the debt; but if the debt is the debt of the person who paid it, or is a debt which he has covenanted to pay, his payment of it raises no right of subrogation, but is simply a performance of his own obligation or covenant.¹ 

The doctrine of subrogation is broad enough to include every instance in which one person, who, not being a mere volunteer, pays a debt which in justice, equity and

§315. Payment of Part of Mortgage Debt. When a third person, at the instance of the mortgagor, pays part of the mortgage debt, but takes no assignment of the mortgage, and no agreement for any, he is not thereby subrogated to the right of the mortgagee as against a subsequent incumbrance; to effect this there must be something more than mere payment and silent receipt of the money by the mortgagee.12

It is sufficient to entitle the third person making the advance for the mortgagor, or other person interested in the property for the payment of a mortgage upon it, that the advance was made upon the promise or reasonable expectation that the mortgage would be assigned as security for the advances.18

I. IN GENERAL. 

§ 320. Ordinary Rule. There can be little doubt as to when an ordinary mortgage given to secure a particular debt payable at a definite time matures, as obviously the mortgage in such a case reaches maturity on default in discharge of the debt. And if no statute interpose, a mortgage securing a debt payable by instalments reaches maturity on default of payment of the first instalment, for the purpose of enforcing payment thereof, and the mortgaged property may be sold therefor. And when the instalments become due before the final hearing, the court may act upon the whole contract. It has been held that a condition in a mortgage that if, at the expiration of the time limited for the payment of the instalments, there should remain due on the mortgage a named sum, the mortgagor might have the privilege of paying the amount due by giving his note therefor, secured by mortgage on other real estate, does not prevent the instalments from falling due at the time stipulated, nor prevent a sale under the mortgage to satisfy them 196

MATURITY 

[§ 321 when due. Where a mortgage is security for interest as well as principal, it reaches maturity for the purpose of foreclosure on default in payment of the interest, in the absence of any special provision on that subject. 

Where a power of sale, in a deed of trust given to secure a note, authorizes the trustee to sell if the note shall not be paid with the interest, the omission to pay interest is a default, and authorizes the trustee to sell. But it has been held that a statute providing that whenever the complaint is filed to foreclose a mortgage upon which there should be due any interest or instalment of principal, on which there are instalments not due, the defendant may pay into court the principal and interest due with costs, and proceedings shall then be stayed, does not authorize the foreclosure of a mortgage before the principal becomes due, where such foreclosure is not authorized by the terms of the mortgage itself. And there is authority for the proposition that an action to foreclose a mortgage for nonpayment of interest cannot be maintained where the mortgage contains no provision for the foreclosure upon such nonpayment. But the rule in 

Michigan is that foreclosure may be brought on failure to pay an instalment of interest.¹ 

§ 321. When Certain Conditions Are Contained in 

Instrument. A mortgage, providing for defeasance in case the mortgagor pays the debts secured within a certain time after notice to him to pay, does not mature until the expiration of such time after the stipulated notice.

The right to foreclose does not accrue, nor does the statute of limitations against that right commence to run, until such time. If the condition of a mortgage is to indemnify the mortgagee against the support of a third person, it is sufficient breach that the mortgagee was compelled to pay for such support for a part of the time, and if there is no place specified where the support 19.

II. VALIDITY AND CONSTRUCTION OF ACCELERATIVE PRO- VISION. 

§ 322. Not in Nature of Penalty. A stipulation in a mortgage providing that the whole debt secured thereby shall become due and payable upon failure of the mortgagor to pay the interest annually or to comply with any other condition of the mortgage is a legal, valid, and enforceable stipulation, and is not in the nature of a penalty or forfeiture. And though a statute authorizing the issue of bonds provides that they are not to mature before a certain time the obligator has a right to mortgage its property for the payment of instalments of interest as well as principal and to make it one of the provisions of the mortgage that it may be foreclosed if these instalments are not paid as they fall due, though a contrary rule has apparently been applied in some instances. 

Accelerative provisions in mortgages are not even viewed with disfavor by the courts, but are to be construed and the intention of the parties ascertained by the same rules as other contracts.

Provisions in a mortgage that default in payment shall mature the entire debt at the option of the holder, and in the note secured by the mortgage, that default shall render the whole sum immediately due and collectible, will be construed together and held to mean that default will render the whole sum due at the option of the creditor. And default in the payment of interest on a note which provides for a payment at stated intervals authorizes immediate foreclosure of the mortgage securing it, although the note provides that interest unpaid when due shall be added to the principal and bear interest, if the mortgage stipulates that in case of default in payment of principal or interest or any part thereof when due the premises may be sold and the whole of the principal and interest, when due or not, retained from the proceeds.* 

§ 324. When Clause Is in Only Note or Mortgage. 

An acceleration clause in the note or bond secured and not in the mortgage, permits the foreclosure of the mortgage according to the terms of such clause. A fortiori is this true where the mortgage is conditioned for the payment of the note or bond according to its true intent and tenor. And it is also usually held that though there be no acceleration clause in the note, an acceleration clause in the mortgage will enable the holder, upon the breach mentioned, to foreclose the mortgage for the full amount of the note, although the debt be not due by its terms. 

Moreover, upon the weight of authority a clause only in the mortgage providing that the debt shall become due upon a contingency therein set forth will mature the note, although it be not due by its terms.5

§ 325. Not Operative Until a Legal Breach Occurs. 

Before the stipulation for the acceleration of the maturity of a mortgage can become operative a legal breach by the mortgagor of the condition on which it is dependent must occur. Thus it has been held that the failure of one who has executed to a nonresident a bond and mortgage in one state upon property therein situated, which fixes no place for payments, to tender interest due at the latter's residence will not entitle the latter to declare the whole debt due for default in payments of interest according to the provisions of the contract, since it is the creditor's duty to provide a place in the former's state where the payments may be made." The mortgagee may be estopped by his conduct, as where he has wrongfully prevented payment, from enforcing an accelerative provision. It has been held that a judgment against a corporation is not collusive in the legal sense, so as to prevent its nonpayment from constituting a default for which a mortgage debt may be declared due under an accelerative provision of the mortgage, merely because the action was undertaken for the purpose of creating such default, if it was brought for a debt that was due and the case was properly conducted. A stipulation in a mortgage given to secure a fixed sum representing the aggregate of the principal of a debt and the interest thereon for the period of the mortgage, that on default by the mortgagor in the performance of certain conditions the whole sum secured shall become due, will not be enforced except upon the cancellation of the unearned interest. § 326. Affirmative Action Must Be Taken. Usually even where a mortgage provides that on failure to perform certain stipulated conditions, the entire debt shall become due, a default does not ipso facto mature the whole debt, but where the maturity of the debt or foreclosure of the mortgage on default is made optional with the mortgagee, some affirmative action must be taken by him evidencing his election to take advantage of the accelerating provision, and until such action has been taken the provision has no operation. Accordingly it is usually held that the mortgagor, after default and at any time before the mortgagee has made manifest his election to accelerate maturity, may properly perform the condition broken, and avoid the consequences of the breach, and cut off the right of the mortgagee subsequently to avail himself thereof to accelerate maturity. 

§ 327. Effect of Affirmative Election. The option to declare the entire debt due on default may be exercised by giving the payor formal notice to the effect that the whole debt is declared to be due, but it is also generally held that the institution of a suit to foreclose for the full amount of the mortgage debt will be notice of the most unequivocal character that the mortgagee wishes to avail himself of his option. There are, however, decisions to the effect that the mortgagee must give notice of his election, and that a demurrer will lie to a complaint in an action to foreclose the mortgage, if it does not show the notice to have been duly given to the mortgagor. Generally speaking, the affirmative exercise by a mortgagee of the option to declare the mortgage due on breach of a stipulated condition brings the mortgage to maturity for all purposes as effectively as if maturity had resulted from lapse of time. Both parties are bound by the elec-

S.) 360 and note, 132 Am. St. Rep. 658. 201

§ 328] tion and neither party can thereafter, without the consent of the other, treat the mortgage as not matured. 

But a provision in a mortgage that the whole sum secured shall become due on any default in payment will not make notes which are not at that time due according to their terms due within the meaning of the rule which gives priority to those first maturing. The priority is to be determined in such a case by the order in which they fall due according to their terms.9 

§ 328. Statute of Limitations. If a mortgage or note provides that upon breach of a stipulated condition, the entire debt, principal and interest, shall at the option of the mortgagee, become immediately due and payable, it is generally held that the provision is merely permissive, and the statute of limitations does not commence to run against the mortgage or debt before the maturity of the principal, unless the mortgagee has exercised his option of declaring its maturity. Where a note provided that, in case of default in the payment of interest, the whole indebtedness should become due if the holder so elected, and the mortgage securing it provided that upon default the whole debt should immediately become due, the stipulation in the note was held governing, and in the absence of an exercise of the option it was held that limitations would not begin to run from a default in the payment of interest, but from the maturity of the note.10

EQUITY OF REDEMPTION.

§ 329] 

 I. NATURE OF EQUITY OF REDEMPTION. 

§ 329. In General. Under the theory of mortgages usually prevalent in this country the mortgagor has an interest in the property mortgaged until he has either disposed of that interest by sale, or until there has been a foreclosure of the mortgage in one of the usual methods of foreclosure. 

§ 330. Distinction Between Right of Redemption and 

Equity of Redemption. A distinction is sometimes made between the right of redemption and equity of redemption. It was held in Lewis v. McBride, 176 Ala. 134, that: 

The equity of redemption is that interest in the land which is held by the mortgagor before foreclosure; while the right of redemption is not an interest in the land at all, but a mere personal privilege given by statute to the mortgagor after the land has been sold under the mortgage. It has been said a valid foreclosure destroys the equity of redemption and creates the right of redemption, but an invalid sale neither destroys the one nor creates the other; no right of redemption exists outside of the statute, and the statute has no extraterritorial force; that the equity of redemption is an interest in the land mortgaged which will descend to the heir of the mortgagor; that the foreclosure under a power of sale in a mortgage has the same effect on the equity of redemption as a strict foreclosure in equity.¹ But in this state there is no clear distinction between the right of redemption and the equity of redemption, indeed the term equity of redemption seems more appropriate after the sale than it does prior to the time of the sale. Prior to the sale the mortgagor has the title to the land, subject to the interest which the mortgagee may have therein and until there has been a forfeiture the mortgagee has no right even to foreclose such mortgage, and after there has been a sale 

1 Jones on Mortgages, 8th Ed., Vol. 2, p. 46, Sec. 774, and cases cited. 204

[§ the interest of the mortgagor is an equitable interest in the land itself, which he may sell or devise, and which only ceases upon his failure to redeem. The right to redeem from a foreclosure at law is a legal right created by the state, and can neither be enlarged nor abridged by the courts.

A redemption is complete when one having the right to redeem pays in proper time to a proper person the sum which was bid with interest from the time of the sale at the rate per cent borne by the mortgage, and, in case such payment is made to the register of deeds, the sum of one dollar as a fee.

Where said amount was paid by the owner to the register of deeds within the proper time, the redemption was complete, and the purchaser at foreclosure sale, who was a stranger to the title, was not thereafter entitled to maintain a bill to create a lien upon said premises to reimburse him for the amount paid after his purchase upon back taxes which were a lien thereon at the time of the foreclosure.

II. WHO MAY REDEEM. 

§ 331. Any Party in Interest. Any person who has an interest in the property, subject to the mortgage, may redeem the same from the effect of such mortgage at any time after the condition of the same has been broken and before the equity of redemption has expired, either before or after foreclosure.

The person seeking to redeem must have an interest derived directly or indirectly from or through the right of the mortgagor. He ought to be an owner of a part of his original equity, or of some interest in it. If he is affected by the mortgage he may redeem; if he is not affected by it, there is no occasion for his redeeming, and he is not allowed to do so.5

§ 332. Joint Plaintiffs. A bill to redeem, filed by several persons jointly, cannot be maintained if the ground of their joint claim fails, whatever any one of them, claiming title from another source, might be entitled to, in a separate proceeding."

If his interest has no connection with the title held by the mortgagor at the time the mortgage was foreclosed, it cannot be made the basis of a right to redeem. Thus it has been held that the purchaser of a tax title has no right to redeem." 

§ 333. Purchaser from Mortgagor. But a purchaser from the mortgagor pending redemption has the right to redeem. The mortgagee's acceptance of the amount due from one who has no right to redeem is in effect a sale of the mortgagee's interest.

Where a mortgagor had left home some months before his mortgage was foreclosed, and his father, who was his heir, being unable to get any trace of his son, executed a deed of the land to another son that he might redeem it, and on the last day of the year for redemption he paid the necessary amount to the register of deeds saying that he redeemed for his brother, if living, if not for himself-in a suit by the purchaser, praying that the deposit of money be decreed to effect no redemption, it was held that the redemption was effectual; for if the mortgagor was living his brother had a right to redeem for him, and, if not, to redeem for himself as the grantee of the mortgagor's heir.8

In case of doubt as to the continued existence of the right to redeem, the law will generally resolve the doubt in favor of the mortgagor and allow redemption.9 

§ 334. Redemption by One Not a Party to the Suit. 

Redemption may be had after foreclosure by any person entitled to redeem who was not made a party to the suit

On a bill to redeem from an invalid foreclosure, the decree should provide for redemption from an unforeclosed security, and not from a void sale; and in determining the amount to be paid, it is erroneous to make a rest in computing interest at the date of the sale.10 

§ 335. Junior Mortgagee. A subsequent mortgagee may redeem from a prior mortgagee at any time after the maturity of a prior mortgage and before the equity of redemption has expired."

Under a contract with a prior mortgagee a subsequent mortgagee may redeem after foreclosure.12 

§ 336. Life Tenant-Reversioner. A tenant for life may redeem; a remainderman or reversioner may also redeem.13 

A life tenant is entitled to the first option and by taking an assignment of the mortgage himself may prevent a redemption by the remainderman. Redemption by a remainderman does not affect the duration of the estate of the life tenant or quicken his own enjoyment thereof. 

A tenant for life of a portion of an estate covered by a mortgage may redeem his interest by paying a proportionate part of the mortgagee's debt if the mortgagee consents. If he redeems the entire estate he is entitled to the possession of the whole until the amount above his proportion is reimbursed to him.

Even if a life tenant and the remaindermen were disseized by sale under lien foreclosure proceedings, where

§ 337. Widow-Married Woman. A widow or a mar ried woman who has joined in a mortgage in release of dower may redeem, for she is entitled to dower as against every person except the mortgagee and those claiming under him. Where the wife was not made a party to foreclosure proceedings and the premises sold for less than the mortgage debt, it was held she could redeem only upon paying the deficiency. This was owing to the peculiar circumstances of this case and could not be stated as a general proposition of law.¹4 14 A widow in bringing a bill in equity to redeem should show that she has no remedy in law to recover her dower, and should therefore set forth that her husband was seized during coverture of only an equity of redemption, or that if he was seized of the legal estate she joined him in the mortgage.

A surety of a debt secured by a junior mortgage upon payment of the debt is entitled by subrogation to the rights of such mortgagee to redeem from a prior mortgagee. And where he mortgages property of his own as collateral security, he is not bound by an agreement between the mortgagor and mortgagee, made without his consent, to apply his property to a satisfaction of the foreclosure decree.15

§ 340. Mortgaged Property Held in Common. A court of equity will not lend its aid to enforce an alleged right to redeem from a mortgage on the land of another, where by the bill complainant appears to be a mere volunteer.18 99 Under our statutes a redemption may be made by "any person lawfully claiming from or under the mortgagor, and so a second mortgagee may redeem from sale under the first mortgage. § 341. Redemption Must Be Entire. It is a well estab lished rule that the mortgage must be entirely redeemed. 

Partial redemption is not permissible; and the rule is the same whether redemption is sought by the mortgagor or by one claiming under or through him. So the whole amount due upon a mortgage must be paid before the mortgaged property can be redeemed by a mortgagor who is a tenant in common with the mortgagee of the mortgaged premises. In like manner a tenant in dower to maintain a bill in equity to redeem land from a mortgage made by her husband and herself, must offer to pay the whole amount due on the mortgage. If a mortgagee of real property refuses to accept payment of a debt and release the mortgage unless paid a bonus to which he is not entitled, and the mortgagor, though protesting, pays the debt with such bonus, such payment is made under duress and an action may be maintained against the mortgagee to recover the amount thereof.80 

In the case of Dayton v. Stahl,21 plaintiff owned one of three tracts included in a first mortgage. Each tract was incumbered with a second mortgage. While foreclosure proceedings of the first and second mortgages on her tract were pending she agreed with the defendant that he should attend the sale under the first mortgage, and bid for the other two tracts until a sum sufficient to satisfy that mortgage was reached, and buy in plaintiff's tract on the sale under the second mortgage, and she would repay him the amount he was required to pay at both sales. Defendant purchased the two tracts at

§ 342. Contribution to Redeem. When the estates of two persons are subject to a common mortgage, which one of them pays for the benefit of both, he has a right to hold the whole estate thus redeemed until the other party shall pay an equitable proportion of the sum paid to redeem, or the party who has paid the incumbrance may in equity enforce contribution from the other. The test by which the right to contribution is always determined is found in the inquiry whether the equities of the parties are equal; if they are equal, the right to contribution exists; but if they are not equal, it does not exist. If as between two parties having the right to redeem one is under obligation to discharge the mortgage and it is paid by the other, he has the right to be subrogated to the rights of the mortgagee.**

III. ACTIONS-PLEADINGS AND PRACTICE ON BILLS TO REDEEM. 

§ 343. Enforcement of Rights After Breach of Condi tion. Where a mortgagor or other person entitled to redeem desires to enforce his right after a breach of the condition by the mortgagor his remedy is by a bill in equity. If the mortgagee is in possession, he has the right to retain the possession until his claim upon the property is paid. So long as the mortgage is in fact 

22 Damm v. Damm, 91 Mich. 424; 

Laylin v. Knox, 41 Mich. 40. 211

§ 343] 

not discharged, and is apparently a subsisting security, the mortgagor cannot obtain possession by ejectment. 

The rule is the same although the mortgagor claims that the debt has been paid in full. So long as the mortgage is apparently unsatisfied, and the mortgagee claims any interest under it, the mortgagor must resort to a suit in equity to redeem; and although he may allege that the mortgage has been paid, or was given for the accommodation of the mortgagee, and may pray that a decree be entered that it be discharged, yet he should at the same time pray that he be allowed to redeem, and should offer to do so if anything be found due upon the mortgage.28

In a bill to redeem the plaintiff must show equities as against the defendant, and that the result of a decree in his favor would, if acted upon by him, be effective. 

In his bill he should offer to pay the amount equitably due from him.

In a recent Michigan case, where there was a foreclosure of a second mortgage, followed by sale, at which the premises were struck off to the mortgagee for the full amount due, and a petition was filed by the receiver of the mortgagor, a bankrupt, five days after the expiration of the period of redemption, praying to intervene in the foreclosure proceedings, and asking to defend therein, and it appearing that a first mortgage upon the same property had been foreclosed and the period of redemption thereunder expired after the filing of said petition, but before hearing, the court said: "Plaintiff contends that the petition is in the nature of a bill to redeem, and that as he filed an answer and cross-bill, consenting to a hearing, and praying an accounting and redemption, petitioner is bound to redeem. While matter set up in the petition might properly have been alleged in a bill to redeem, the petition is not a bill to redeem. It has neither prayer for redemption nor offer

§343a. Application of Payments. Where neither party has made application of a payment the court will apply it to the oldest item, especially where the proceeding is in equity and such application will prevent the working of a forfeiture.

In a suit by a mortgagor to be relieved from the foreclosure of a mortgage, where it appears that after the foreclosure by advertisement for nonpayment of interest, of which the mortgagor was unaware, he paid more than enough to redeem, although no application thereof was made, the court below properly applied the said payment to redeem from the foreclosure and the balance on the mortgage debt, which in the meantime had become due, and fixed the time within which payment thereof should be made, but which, because of appeal, had become inoperative, and a new date was therefore fixed.280

IV. AS TO THE TIME FOR REDEMPTION. 

§ 345. What Law Governs. In the different states the laws differ as to the time after a sale or from the date when suit has commenced within which a party interested may redeem from the effects of the mortgage or a sale thereon. In Michigan under a power of sale where one is included within the terms of mortgage, the mortgagor or other party having a right to redeem, may redeem from a sale within twelve months from the date of the deed upon the foreclosure sale; and where proceedings are had in equity the sale cannot be ordered within six months from the date when such proceedings are begun and redemption can be made from the sale at any time within six months after such sale. A mortgage of land in one state to a building and loan association organized in another state where payment and performance are to be made is a contract under the laws of the latter state and is governed by the laws of that state. 25 

§ 346. When After Statutory Period. Redemption may be allowed after the expiration of the statutory period if it appears that the mortgagor understood that the purchaser at the foreclosure sale took the title in 

24 Lindow v. Webber, 125 Mich. 

641; Cady v. Burgess, 144 Mich. 523. 

25 Home Savings & Loan Ass'n v. Mason, 127 Mich. 676. 214

[§ order to allow him to redeem, and that therefore he gave up efforts to obtain the money elsewhere.26 

But if the mortgagor afterward abandons his design to redeem, and takes leases of the property from the purchaser at the foreclosure sale his right to redeem is lost. 

The right of a second mortgagee to redeem cannot be prejudiced by an extension of the statutory time of redemption by arrangement between the first mortgagee and the mortgagor.27

Where a mortgagor, after a mortgage had been foreclosed, made an agreement with the mortgagees for the execution of a new mortgage on the premises, after the period of redemption had expired, and he was led thereby to permit the redemption period to expire without redeeming, and thereafter the mortgagees refused to carry out such agreement the mortgagor would be entitled to equitable relief on the ground of fraud. 

Where the mortgagor had deeded certain lots from the mortgaged premises and his vendees had been assured by the mortgagee, after he had acquired the property upon foreclosure, that they could go on making their payments after the redemption period had expired the same as before, and in reliance thereon they made no effort to redeem 'and where the mortgagees thereafter refused to carry out said agreement the court held that the lot holders, plaintiffs in subsequent proceedings, were entitled to equitable relief.7 § 347. Since the passage of the Statute of 1843, above mentioned, except in certain instances covered by a recent statute hereinafter mentioned, the Michigan Supreme Court has held firmly against any attempt upon the part of the mortgagee, even by the consent of the mortgagor, given at the time when the mortgage is executed, exercising any rights of ownership over the property until after sale upon foreclosure has become absolute. 

In an early case 28b the Michigan Supreme Court held that a mortgage, which in its terms granted to the mortgagee not only the premises, but also all rents, income, and profits, did not permit the mortgagee to dispossess the mortgagor during the period of foreclosure. The only exception to this rule has been in cases where the mortgagor has abandoned the mortgaged property, or has permitted waste to the extent that it is injurious to the interests of all parties concerned in the mortgaged property.

§ 350. Lapse of Time as Affecting Right of Redemp tion. The right to redeem from a mortgage after default, being of equitable cognizance, may be lost by laches, even in the absence of a statute of limitations. 

Except where a mortgagor is under a disability, as provided in the statute of limitations, fifteen years' possession by the mortgagee, without any account or acknowledgment of the mortgage, bars the equity of redemption and redemption has been refused after the lapse of less period, but the period is fixed at fifteen years in Michigan. Furthermore, the right to redeem property from a mortgage is barred by the same period which bars the right to foreclose the mortgage, as well in the case of deeds absolute intended as security as in the case of mortgages generally. The receipt, by a mortgagee in possession, of the rents and profits of the land is not such a payment as will prevent the running of the statute of limitations against the right to redeem from the mortgage, and the right of action for the redemption of mortgaged property from the lien of a mortgage, when barred by the statute of limitations, cannot be revived by an offer of the mortgagor to pay the debt. However, the possession of a mortgagee under his mortgage is not

V. FURTHER SUGGESTIONS AS TO REDEMPTION OF MORTGAGE. 

§ 351. What Law Governs. It is to be noted that the right to redeem land from a mortgage or absolute deed given as security is governed by the law of the place where the land lies, and consequently a rule there prevailing that such right is barred when an action on the debt is barred must govern, although in another state where the parties reside and the contract was made the fact that an action on the debt was barred would not defeat the right to redeem. Right cannot be enlarged or curtailed. The right to redeem from a foreclosure-at-law is a legal right created by the statute and can neither be enlarged nor abridged by the courts.38

When the mortgaged property is sold by the purchaser at a mortgage sale before the equity of redemption expires the vendor acquires the rights of the mortgage sale purchaser and his title becomes complete if there is no redemption within the statutory period.34 

§ 352. Redemption of Mortgage for Support. Where the condition of a mortgage calls for the support of the mortgagee, or some other person, the land cannot be redeemed by the payment of a sum of money.

Generally a mortgage given to secure the performance of any act or condition other than the payment of money can only be satisfied by the performance of such act or condition and unless the instrument states an amount to be fixed damages for a breach of such condition such mortgage after foreclosure could only be redeemed by the payment of an amount to be determined by the court from the evidence as to injury suffered by the breach.

I. INDEPENDENT ACTION AT LAW. 

§ 353. Collateral Security. The taking of collateral security for the payment of a debt does not afford any implication that the creditor is to look to it only or primarily for the payment of the debt. The obligation of the debtor to respond in his person and property is usually the same as if no security had been given. Therefore, a creditor holding a note secured by a mortgage may ignore his security and bring an action on the note. The promise to pay, as evidenced by a promissory note is one distinct agreement, and, if couched in proper terms, is negotiable, while the pledge of real estate to secure that promise as evidenced by a mortgage is another distinct agreement, which is not intended to affect in the least the promise to pay, but only to provide a remedy for the failure of performance. However, leave to proceed at law while foreclosure is pending in chan- 227

§ 354] 

cery ought not to be granted ex parte where the defendant is within reach.¹ 

§ 354. Independent Action on Note. Under the stat utes of some states no action can be maintained for the recovery on a promissory note secured by mortgage unless the action be coupled with an action to foreclose the mortgage, except where it is shown that the security has become valueless. The constitutionality of such statutes has, however, been attacked, and it has been held that a statute limiting the right to enforce a debt secured by mortgage to the property mortgaged is an undue restraint on the liberty of a citizen to contract with respect to his property rights. Furthermore, under such a law, a man who holds a promissory note for which mortgage security had been originally taken is not, on the loss or depreciation of that security, given the same rights as another citizen who simply took a promissory note without any security. Proceeding at law, without leave, while a foreclosure in chancery is pending, is an abuse of practice; but it does not invalidate the judgment which may be affirmed with costs without prejudice to relief below against the wrongful procedure.

ENFORCEMENT OF MORTGAGE RIGHTS [§ 356 $355. Where Property Has Been Converted Into 

Money. It is a general principle that when either real or personal property, on which there is an outstanding mortgage, is turned into money, the rights of the mortgagee continue unaltered. The court will direct the application of the money according to the rights of the parties as they existed prior to the conversion of the property into money. This rule applies where property is appropriated under eminent domain proceedings. But generally speaking where property subject to a prior mortgage is sold under execution, the purchaser buys subject to the lien. The lien is not divested by the sale. 

The mortgagee, under this rule, has no right to the proceeds of the sale, since his lien on the property continues to subsist in full force. However, by the concurrent consent of the mortgagor, the mortgagee, and the levying creditor, the sale may be of the entire interest in the property. Then the proceeds may be applied to the payment of the unforeclosed mortgage according to its priority. And a like course is pursued when the mortgagee is otherwise remediless. 

§ 356. Disposition of Property by Public Authorities, etc. When land is turned into money by some act of the public authorities, the general rule is that the lien of one who had a mortgage on the premises extends to the money, and the lien of the mortgagee may be enforced by equitable process on the principle in equity that one who has a lien on property may follow the proceeds and enforce his lien thereon if there is no remedy at law. So, where mortgaged property is appropriated under eminent domain proceeding, the mortgagee has a claim to the award. Construing statutes providing that in case of a tax sale the collector may sell the whole or any part of the land, and after satisfying the taxes and charges shall pay the balance to the owner of the estate on demand, it has been held that the word "owner" does not include a mortgagee not in possession, if his

1 interest has not been assessed to him as real estate, but that he has an equitable lien on the proceeds of the land, which he can enforce by equitable process.*

II. STRICT FORECLOSURE. 

§ 357. The Natural Remedy. A strict foreclosure was the remedy upon a mortgage when it was regarded as a conditional sale of the land, rather than as a mere security. The mortgagor having failed to perform the condition it was consistent with this doctrine of the mortgage that the courts after having relieved the mortgagor from the forfeiture on account of his failure to perform the condition should require him to perform it within a reasonable time, or be forever barred of his right to redeem, but when the mortgage came to be regarded as a mere security for the payment of the debt the breach of the condition is of no effect beyond giving the mortgage creditor the right to resort to his security. The natural remedy for the breach was to sell the property secured and apply the proceeds to the payment of the debt. In this way the debtor would have the benefit of the estate when this was of greater value than the debt and the mortgagee would have a claim for the deficiency not paid by the proceeds of sale. The advantages of the sale of the property over a foreclosure were discussed in the earlier cases before the principle of ordering a sale had become almost universal." § 358. Foreclosure in Michigan. A mortgage can be foreclosed only in equity or by advertisement.

III. FORECLOSURE BY ADVERTISEMENT. 

§ 359. Statutory Provisions. It is provided by the statutes, that every mortgage of real estate containing not been expressly overruled by our supreme court, yet in more recent cases the court has laid down the rule stated in the text. 

In Sanborn v. Sanborn, 104 

Mich. 180, the court says: "It follows that the deed was in fact a mortgage and the only proper remedy for the defendant was by a bill in chancery to foreclose it." 

In Kollen v. Sooy, 172 Mich. 214, the court says: "Mortgages can only be foreclosed by statutory publication or by a foreclosure suit. Equity has jurisdiction only pursuant to statutory provisions.” 

In Maginn v. Cashin, 196 Mich. 

221, in a case in which what purported to be a deed absolute upon its face was declared to be a mortgage, the court said: "The holder as assignee of the mortgage could not foreclose same by merely declaring the contract forfeited.' 

In this case it was held that a deed given by a son to his mother as security for her endorsement of his personal note with a land contract from the mother to the son, constituting a mortgage between the parties, continued to be such even against one to whom the mother subsequently deeded the property. However, this deed was given by the mother to her daughter, and while it is not expressly stated that she knew of the nature of the transaction between the mother and her son there might be a strong presumption of that fact from the relation of the parties. 

In Carveth v. Winegar, 133 

Mich. 34, the court held: "That a defendant in a bill to declare a deed a mortgage who, as a subsequent purchaser made improvements in good faith in reliance upon his title was entitled to compensation, and his rights were directed to be protected upon an accounting." 

The person thus protected had only a one-half interest in the property. He claimed that he did not have notice of the fact that the deed was given as a mortgage.

He was brother to the party to whom the deed was given who had deeded the one-half interest to him. It would seem if he had been a purchaser in good faith of a one-half interest without notice of the true condition of the title and in the belief that the deed was what it purported to be, an absolute conveyance of the title to the property, he would have not only the right to compensation but whatever advantage might be gained by acquiring the title to the property. In this case the question as to recording of the deed as a mortgage does not seem to be involved.

ENFORCEMENT OF MORTGAGE RIGHTS [§ 360 § 360. Further Decisions-Under the Michigan Statute for Foreclosure by Advertisement. A foreclosure of a mortgage by advertisement is valid only when the mortgage contains a power of sale.22

The recital in a sheriff's deed, if the mortgage contains a power of sale, is the evidence of that fact.28 

In foreclosures of mortgages by advertisement substantial compliance with the statute is required.24 It is an ex parte nonjudicial proceeding based on contract and authorized by the mortgagor, and, while it should not be hampered by unreasonable construction of the statute, all of its essentials must be complied with. In such proceeding no personal notice is required under the power of sale, either at common law or by statute, the only other requirement besides the publication being the posting of a notice upon a conspicuous place upon the premises.

Where such sale is fair, on its face, with all statutory requirements fully complied with, plaintiffs, in a suit to set aside such foreclosure on the ground of fraudulent and unfair conduct, have the burden of proof to establish the invalidity thereof.a

A statutory foreclosure sale is invalid if the notice of sale does not give the mortgagor's name correctly, but a notice of foreclosure of a mortgage by advertisement, which incorrectly gives the date of the instrument, is not fatally defective, where it describes the date, volume, and page of the record of the mortgage. 

There must be reasonable certainty in foreclosure by advertisement so that there will be no confusion on the part of prospective purchasers, and so that when they bid they may know, with exercise of ordinary intelligence, what property is offered.25a

I. PROCEDURE. 

§ 361. Nature of the Action. A foreclosure suit has been said to be merely a proceeding for the legal determination of the existence of the mortgage lien, the ascertainment of its extent, and the subjection to a sale of the estate pledged for its satisfaction. It necessarily presupposes a subsisting, living mortgage, with a correlative right of redemption, not already in any manner cut off, barred, or extinguished. In order to establish a ground of recovery against a defendant who does not claim under the maker of the mortgage, the plaintiff is required to show that the mortgagor had title to the property, so that the mortgage created a lien. An action will lie to foreclose a mortgage against the estate of a deceased mortgagor, although the debt secured by the mortgage has been presented and duly allowed. Likewise, a foreclosure may be had against one of several joint mortgagors, where, after executing the mortgage, they partition the land, agree each to pay a specified portion of the mortgage, and one of them does pay his share, and secures a release as to his portion. And when several persons are interested in lands encumbered by a mortgage, whether that interest be as owners of distinct parcels of the land or as tenants in common of the whole, the mortgagee is not, in general, obliged to take notice of their separate and distinct interest, but on the nonpayment of the mortgage money is entitled to a decree of foreclosure against all of them jointly.¹ 

1 Hubbard v. Ascutney Mill Dam 

Co., 20 Vt. 402, 50 Am. Dec. 41. 

See Spear v. Hadden, 31 Mich. 265. 242

[§ Under Michigan laws no provision is made for proceedings subsequent to a valid decree, sale, confirmation, and expiration of the redemption period." § 362. Waiver. Although there is some authority to the contrary, the general rule is that the institution of an independent action on a note or bond is not a waiver of the right to foreclose the mortgage. An agreement by a mortgagee not to take advantage of foreclosure for a given time is binding, and waives the forfeiture and opens the foreclosure. But a mortgagee having an option by the terms of the mortgage to foreclose on default in stipulated conditions does not, by mere delay in bringing an action after default, waive his right to foreclose, unless the mortgagor is prejudiced by the delay, though the option may be lost by a subsequent performance by the latter of the condition broken. A waiver of the right to foreclose for breach of a covenant or condition cannot be taken advantage of unless pleaded.

The question has sometimes been raised as to the effect of receiving a payment upon a mortgage subsequent to the beginning of foreclosure proceedings, and it has been held in certain instances that the proceedings to foreclose were made void by the mortgagee's receiving such a payment.

There is no question but that if such a payment is made with the agreement between the person making the same and the mortgagee that the foreclosure proceedings would be abandoned or that the time for redemption would be extended, the mortgage would thereafter be estopped to insist that the foreclosure proceedings were in full force or that the equity of redemption expired contrary to such understanding.a However, where part payments are made after foreclosure by ad-

Trust Co., 243 Mich. 451.

Co., 20 Vt. 402, 50 Am. Dec. 41. 

See Spear v. Hadden, 31 Mich. 265. 

3a Dodge v. Brewer, 31 Mich. 227. 18 243

§ 363] 

vertisement and received with a clear understanding that the redemption was to be completed by paying the whole sum necessary for that purpose within the year allowed by statute, such payments would be in affirmance and not in avoidance of the sale, and their acceptance would not operate as a waiver of the foreclosure.b

An agreement between the purchaser of the premises at a statutory foreclosure and the mortgagors, whereby the period of redemption was for a valid consideration extended six months, such consideration to be retained as compensation for the use of the land in case of a failure to redeem, would be sustained and would not have the effect of voiding the foreclosure sale or of extending the time of redemption beyond the six months provided for in such agreement.³ 

Where contract purchaser from the mortgagor after a mortgage foreclosure sale arranged with the mortgagee, which was the bidder at such sale, that he should make payments to such bidder toward redemption, and where he paid $600 toward such redemption, the foreclosure was not waived by such partial payment because as it was held by the court, while it may be waived by agreement no intention to waive appeared in the particular instance from the arrangements made.d $363. Process and Jurisdiction. In foreclosure proceedings, due service of process is no less required to give a court jurisdiction of the person and subject matter than in ordinary personal actions. Thus where the subsequent incumbrancers are necessary parties, it is not sufficient merely to serve on them a copy of the bill to foreclose. They must be regularly brought in by the service of process or their rights will not be affected by the proceedings. However, a foreclosure proceeding may be prosecuted just as successfully on substituted

Substituted Service. Where service is made by publication the laws of Michigan provide: "Whenever a bill shall be filed in chancery, for relief, or for the benefit of the creditors generally of any person, or of any estate, or for the benefit of any other persons than the plaintiff, who will come in and contribute to the expense of such suit, every order which may be made thereon requiring such creditors or other persons to exhibit their demands shall in all cases be published once in each week, for at least three weeks, and as much longer as the court may direct, in any newspaper which the court may designate. "If the bill shall have been filed to procure the foreclosure or satisfaction of a mortgage, the court, instead of proceeding to a sequestration, may decree a sale of the mortgaged premises, or of such part thereof as may be necessary to discharge the mortgage, and the costs of suit, as in other cases. Service of process upon the filing of a cross-bill would be necessary upon all cross-defendants, excepting the plaintiff. 

§ 364. Jurisdiction Over Land in Another State. It is a fundamental principle of jurisprudence that a judgment or decree cannot operate extraterritorially so as to affect the title to land in another state or country, and therefore it is beyond the power of any court to render a binding judgment in foreclosure proceedings as to land located in another state. It does not follow, however, that under no circumstances can a mortgagee obtain relief without resort to the courts of the state or country in which the mortgaged land lies. If the court to which he applies obtains jurisdiction of the person of the defendant, it may decree foreclosure and sale of the land, though situated within a foreign jurisdiction, and while the land cannot be sold under and by virtue of the decree the court may enforce the decree 

5 Emery v. Airth, 180 Mich. 433. 246

[§ indirectly by compelling the defendant to convey the mortgaged property. But the court should not exercise this power except under unusual circumstances and when it is necessary in order to prevent loss or to protect the rights of the mortgagee; in all other cases he should be required to resort to the remedies of. courts of the jurisdiction in which the land is situated." 

II. GENERAL PRINCIPLES IN RELATION TO PARTIES. 

§ 365. All Parties Claiming Through Mortgagor or 

Mortgagee. One of the leading purposes of a suit to foreclose a mortgage is to secure such a decree as will enable the plaintiff to sell all the right and title that his mortgage covers, and enable a purchaser at the sale to ascertain what title it is that he buys. To attain this end it is usually necessary that all claims held against the mortgaged premises should be adjusted. Ordinarily therefore all persons who are beneficially interested either in the estate mortgaged or the demand secured are proper parties to a suit to foreclose. This rule, generally, will only embrace the mortgagor and the mortgagee, and those who have acquired rights or interests under them in the mortgagor's estate; for these are the only persons having any rights or obligations growing out of the mortgage, or interested in any manner in the subject matter of the action. A stranger claiming adversely to the title of the mortgagor as he is not affected by the mortgage, is in no way interested in the foreclosure suit. 

It can make no difference to him whether the mortgage is valid or invalid, whether it be discharged or foreclosed, whether the estate mortgaged, the only estate which can be affected by the decree, remains in the mortgagor, or is transferred to another. Joint mortgagees whose debts are several may join in a bill to foreclose. 

In fact, the action should be brought by all where their 

6 Richard v. Boyd, 124 Mich. 

396; Clark v. Chapman, 215 Mich. 

518; C. L. '29 (13997, Sub. 12). 247

§ 366] 

interest is joint, but if they refuse to unite as plaintiffs, those who refuse to join should be made defendants.a 

So wards are necessary parties to a suit by the joint mortgagee, to foreclose a mortgage made to secure money due them. It seems though, that an action by one mortgagee to enforce his claim has been allowed, but the rights of the other mortgagees were not affected if they were not made parties to the action. In actions on instalment notes where the liens are pro rated some authorities rule that the holders of the different notes should be made parties plaintiff, or on refusal to join should be made parties defendant; but where the plaintiff foreclosing for an instalment has a priority it seems that the holder of the other notes is not a necessary party plaintiff, but should be made a party defendant in order to give the purchaser a good title and to bar the claims of the holders of the several notes." 

§ 366. Questions of Title Cannot Be Litigated. The great weight of authority holds that in an action to foreclose a mortgage questions of title, adverse, or paramount, cannot be litigated, and that consequently adverse claimants are neither necessary nor proper parties to a foreclosure suit.

It is not competent in a foreclosure suit, to litigate the right of a party who sets up a legal title which, if valid, is adverse and paramount to the title of both mortgagor and mortgagee. However, the determination of the exact amount due on the mortgage, which involved the determination of the precise amount of a payment, is imperatively involved in a foreclosure suit.⁹ 

In a suit to foreclose a mortgage containing a stipulation that the collateral note is not to be paid until the payee at his own expense shall obtain a release of an apparent dower right or that it shall otherwise cease to exist, it is

[§ competent for the court to pass on the question of such dower right, on the ground of which a defense is made, although the person in whom it is claimed to exist is not, and could not regularly be made a party to the action.10 Where a subsequent purchaser of the mortgaged premises from the mortgagor has, in order merely to perfect his title of record, procured quitclaim deeds from the mortgagor's grantors, under such circumstances as would render it fraudulent for him to set up such conveyances as a title adverse and paramount to that of the mortgagor, the mortgagor under proper allegations in his foreclosure bill, may have such adverse title declared null and void." A suit to foreclose a mortgage cannot be instituted merely for the purpose of determining the adverse claim of defendant, holding under foreclosure of a mortgage executed by complainant's grantor prior to the mortgage in suit.12 In an action to foreclose a mortgage on land, and buildings removed therefrom without the mortgagee's consent, where the purchaser of the buildings is made a defendant by reason of his claim to the buildings as purchaser from the mortgagor, the rights of the complainant to a lien on the buildings may be determined. It is not a litigation of the title to mortgaged property in foreclosure proceedings. 18 

The mortgagee when seeking to foreclose his mortgage should endeavor to have all parties whose interests are identical with his own, join with him in such proceedings, but if he is unable to get any party who would be a proper party plaintiff to join with him he can make such party a party defendant. The only proper or necessary parties to a foreclosure suit are the mortgagor and the mortgagee and those who have acquired rights or interests under them subsequent to the mortgage.

 III. PARTIES PLAINTIFF. 

§ 367. Who Are Parties. If several persons are made mortgagees, or are entitled to the mortgage money, all of them must be parties to the suit, and as stated above, unless they will join as plaintiffs, such as will not join should be made parties defendant. A bill to foreclose a mortgage must be brought under the jurisdiction in which the property or a portion of the same is situated.14 

In general, the party entitled to foreclose is the actual creditor who is the real and beneficial owner of the debt secured and who is entitled to receive the money due.15 

§ 368. The Assignee of a Mortgage. In general the assignee of a mortgage should bring the suit for foreclosure in his own name. A form of assignments, which is unconditional and which transfers the real and beneficial ownership of the securities to the assignee, will entitle him to maintain a bill for foreclosure.16 Where an assignment is made for the purpose of securing a debt as collateral security and the mortgagee has a pledgor's interest in the mortgage he should be made a party to the suit by the assignee to foreclose it, although the assignment be in terms absolute and recites payment of a full consideration for it. The same would apply in any instance where the assignor has an interest in the mortgage. 

§ 369. Assignment Pending Foreclosure. If a mort gage has been assigned, the assignee should maintain the suit to foreclose the mortgage; and even if the assignment is made pending a foreclosure suit by the mortgagee, the assignee may generally be substituted as plaintiff. If such assignee is not made a party, the bill must be dismissed.17 An assignment pendente lite can-

(Mich.) 416. 250

[§ not, however, affect the proceedings on the decree, unless it appears of record or is brought to the knowledge of the court.18 

§370. Assignee of Mortgage Note. The mortgage note is the initial instrument and the mortgage itself a mere incident of it; consequently a transfer of the note or other evidence of the debt carries with it the security without a special assignment of it. Therefore, a suit to foreclose the mortgage may be brought by the assignee of the note or debt without making the mortgagee who assigned it a party.18 It has also been held that the assignee of notes who acquires a mortgage subsequently executed to secure the notes is entitled to foreclose the mortgage. Where there are a number of notes secured by the same mortgage and the notes are held by different parties all of such parties should be made parties to the suit, or a suit should be brought in the name of some person acting as trustee for the holders of the several notes secured by the mortgage. 

It has been held, however, that where a mortgage secures several debts or claims held by different mortgagees, or several notes which have passed to different holders, any one of such mortgagees or holders may proceed alone to foreclose the mortgage.20

It has also been held that two holders of notes cannot join as plaintiffs to enforce the mortgage; that there is no community of interest between such holders, but rather an antagonism; that only one such holder can be plaintiff, and that he must make the other holders defendants, so that the amounts and priorities of their several liens may be determined.

§ 371. Partners. A partner who holds a mortgage as security for a debt due the partnership should join the other partners with him as plaintiffs in an action to foreclose it. If one partner brings suit alone he may amend by joining his copartners. It has been held in Michigan that it is immaterial whether a partner who holds a mortgage as trustee for the partnership joins his partners or not.22

When a mortgage secures an indebtedness due to the mortgagees jointly, their interest in the estate so far partakes of the nature of the debt that the doctrine of survivorship applies, and the suit to foreclose may be brought in the name of the survivor, without making the heir or personal representatives of the deceased mortgagee a party.23 

§ 372. Survivor of Joint Assignees. It has been held that the survivor of joint assignees of a mortgage may collect the indebtedness by suit or otherwise. The early decisions in Michigan are to the effect that there is no right of survivorship in the title to the mortgagee's interest in the indebtedness, or the mortgaged property, and if the surviving joint mortgagee shall collect the indebtedness he will be required to account to the representatives of the deceased joint mortgagee's estate for his proportion of the amount collected.24

However, parties may create joint tenancies in personal property by express contract, the Statutes of Michigan nowhere forbidding it, and there being nothing immoral or against the public good in such contracts, and therefore, a real estate mortgage running to a husband and wife, "as joint tenants, with sole right to the survivor," has been held to create a joint tenancy with a

[§ 374a right of survivorship in the wife on the death of the husband.24€ § 373. Trustees. It is a general rule that a nominal trustee cannot bring the suit in his own name alone, but must join with him the names of those persons who have the beneficial interest. But where, on account of the number of the persons interested, great inconvenience and expense would be incurred in joining them in the bill, the court will in its discretion dispense with a strict adherence to this rule. Where a mortgage is made or assigned to the cashier of a bank, not as an individual, but as an officer of the bank, he is not a necessary party in an action by the bank to foreclose the mortgage; for the mortgage shows that it is a contract with the bank.25 

§ 374. 

Foreign Receivers. When a foreign receiver is obliged to invoke the aid of the court of another state in asserting his title to assets within its jurisdiction, such court will not, in the exercise of comity, recognize his title to the prejudice of the citizens of its own state, who have fairly acquired title to the assets, either by purchase, attachment, or other legal process, or whose claims are entitled to priority as equitable liens.26 

§ 374a. Foreign Corporations. A mortgagor is not entitled to cancel a mortgage in equity on the ground that mortgagee, a foreign corporation, was not licensed to do business in this state where his bill contains no offer to do equity. § 375. Beneficiaries and Trustees. If a cestui que trust, or other holder of the mortgage debt, brings a bill to foreclose, the trustee is an indispensable party, because it is more particularly the legal estate that is affected by the decree of foreclosure and sale, and in case of redemption the trustee is the one to release the property. The trustee and the beneficiary should unite as plaintiffs.27 

§ 376. Executor, Administrator or Devisee. Upon the death of the mortgagee or of a mortgage trustee, the right of action upon the mortgage securities is in his executor or administrator, and not in the heirs of the mortgagee. Of course the mortgagee may, by his will, settlement, or otherwise, provide that the mortgage security shall go to his heir as devisee; and then the right of the heir to sue rests upon the authority so given. One to whom a specific mortgage is bequeathed for life may maintain a bill to foreclose it, although there be a further bequest over to another of the remainder after the death of the first taker.28

Such immediate legatee is entitled to the possession of the securities, and as well to the possession of the proceeds of the same upon collection. It is necessary that such holder of securities should have the authority to convert them into money in order to obtain the income and protect the property from loss.29 

§ 377. Mortgage to Executor or Guardian. A mort gage made to an executor or guardian should be foreclosed by such person in his official capacity. Since it is a guardian's duty to collect the debts due his ward, by

29 Sutphen v. Ellis, 35 Mich. 446. 254

[§ suit if necessary, the guardian is the proper party to maintain proceedings for foreclosure of the ward's mortgage. Where a mortgage has been made to a guardian or administrator and the estate has been settled and the property or securities turned over to the heir, or to the ward, the heir or ward, as the case may be, will be the proper person to maintain a suit for foreclosure. 

IV. PARTIES DEFENDANT. 

§ 378. Mortgagor Who Has Conveyed Title. It is generally held that where a mortgagor has conveyed all of his interest in mortgaged premises, and retains the equity of redemption no longer, he is not a necessary party to a suit for the foreclosure of the mortgage if no personal judgment is sought, though a contrary rule obtains if personal judgment is sought or if his deed of conveyance contains a covenant of warranty against all incumbrances.31 § 379. Grantee of Mortgagor. A grantee of the mortgagor should be made a party to a foreclosure proceeding else his title will not be affected. Accordingly, it has been held that a grantee of the mortgaged lands has a right to be heard on the validity and extent of the lien, and no valid decree for a sale can pass until this right has been afforded to him.32 

§ 380. Adverse or Paramount Title. It has some times been held that a claimant of title paramount to a mortgage is a proper party to a suit to foreclose it, and, if the decree is against him, it is conclusive of his claim

of title. But the weight of authority affirms that persons claiming the mortgaged premises by title adverse and paramount to that of the mortgagor are neither necessary nor proper parties defendant in a foreclosure suit. The rights of such parties, as a rule, are not affected either where they are made parties or where they are omitted.88 

§ 381. Prior Lien Holders. It is a general rule that persons holding liens prior to the mortgage under foreclosure are neither necessary nor proper parties to the action, because the only proper object of the proceedings is to bar all rights subsequent to the mortgage; and the decree can have no effect on the rights of parties having priority, whether they are made parties to the action or not. It seems, however, that there is some authority to the contrary. And it has been said that a prior lien holder is a proper though not an indispensable party. 

§ 382. Subsequent Lien Holders. The question as to the necessity of making a junior incumbrancer a party to a suit to foreclose a senior mortgage is involved in some confusion, which for the most disappears when the distinction is observed between that question as affecting the jurisdiction of the court as to the proper practice to be pursued in foreclosure proceedings, and as affecting the barring or cutting off of the junior lien. By the great weight of authority, a junior mortgagee or incumbrancer is not a necessary party to a proceeding at law or in equity to foreclose a real estate mortgage, so far as concerns the jurisdiction of the court to render a decree of foreclosure binding on all the parties to the proceeding, 83 Dickerson v. Carter, 94 U. S. 734, 24 L. Ed. 136. 256

[§ though he is a necessary party in order to foreclose and bar any right to redemption he has in the property by virtue of his lien. So, where the senior mortgagee knows that a junior mortgagee has assigned his mortgage, or where the assignee of a junior mortgage has recorded his assignment, the assignee is a necessary party to a suit to foreclose the senior mortgage to entitle the holder of the senior mortgage to a decree cutting off and barring the rights of the holder of the junior mortgage in the mortgaged premises.35 §383. Wife; Husband. A wife has, through her husband, an interest in all real property of which he is seized during the marriage, and is therefore a proper party to an action to foreclose a mortgage executed by him on such property. And where she has joined in the mortgage, it becomes necessary that she be joined in the suit. 

Otherwise, the foreclosure will stand for nothing as against her. Certainly a wife is a necessary party where she holds the legal title to the property. And it has been said that a judgment to which a wife is not a party foreclosing a mortgage on the homestead, though her rights accrued after the execution of the mortgage, is void as against her, and a purchaser at the sale thereunder acquires no title whatever. But the wife, where the mortgage is given for the purchase money of land sold, is not a necessary party to a bill to foreclose the mortgage. 

In such case, the seizin of the husband passes from him the instant that he acquires it, and being immediately revested in the grantor, the widow cannot claim dower in the premises. If then the widow would not be endowable, the wife, while her husband is living, can have no interest in the premises, and consequently she need not be a party to the foreclosure. It has been held that the husband of one in possession of land claiming title is a

§ 385. Equitable Owner. The equities of a grantor in an absolute deed who retains an unrecorded defeasance are postponed only to the lien on the subsequent mortgage of his grantee without notice, and cannot be extinguished or foreclosed by a suit to which he is not a party.

Where the mortgaged property is subject to a trust in favor of third persons, they should be made parties to a suit to foreclose and a decree against the trustee alone does not bind them.88 A statutory provision permitting the trustees of an express trust to sue without joining the cestui que trust does not apply in case of an attempted foreclosure of a deed of trust given to secure the claims of different parties, to determine to whose interest an accounting is necessary; but all the beneficiaries should be made parties to the action. § 386. Occupants, etc. 

Occupants, etc. Where a tenant in common has mortgaged his undivided interest in the common land, and a voluntary partition is afterwards made between himself and his cotenants, he releasing to them his interest in the part assigned to them the mortgage remains a lien at law on their part, and they are necessary parties to a suit for foreclosure. Likewise, one in possession of real estate under claim of right from a mortgagor is a necessary party to a foreclosure of the mortgage, and a decree of foreclosure is not effective as to him unless he is joined. Likewise, generally a lessee is held to be a necessary party to a foreclosure proceeding involving the lands held by him; and as a usual thing he will not be affected by the decree unless he has been made a party. 

One who has purchased nursery trees under an execution against a mortgagor appears not to be a necessary party to the foreclosure of a mortgage previously made on the lands on which the trees grew. A purchaser in possession under an unrecorded deed should be made a party.39 

§ 387. Personal Representatives, etc. The personal representatives of a deceased mortgagor are indispensable parties to a foreclosure. Likewise, the personal representatives of the deceased assignee of a prior undischarged mortgage are proper parties defendant to a suit to foreclose a second mortgage. The heirs of a mortgagor should be made parties to a foreclosure action.40

 § 388. Remedy for Improper Omission. If a mortgage is foreclosed without making a junior mortgagee a party, he may, notwithstanding the decree and the sale file his bill against the purchaser to redeem from such senior incumbrance thereby becoming subrogated to the rights and interests of the original mortgagee; and he generally has also the privilege of prosecuting a proceeding for the foreclosure of the mortgage, without reference to the foreclosure of the senior mortgage, except that he should join as a party the purchaser under the senior mortgage, as the foreclosure should, of course, be subject to the prior claim of the senior mortgagee.

But where the junior mortgagee, though not made a party to a proceeding has knowledge of the proceeding and omits to give notice of his rights, a court of equity, in the exercise of a sound discretion, may properly deny to him the right to have a sale set aside as against the purchaser, who was ignorant of the existence of the junior mortgage, and limit his relief to redemption."1

V. INTERVENTION. 

§ 389. Who May Intervene. A party having any inter est in the premises who would be affected by a decree in suit pending may ask leave to intervene, either as a plaintiff or a defendant in such cause. If his interests are not identical with those of the plaintiff he should ask to intervene as a defendant, even though his interests are antagonistic to other defendants in the cause. He would be permitted, if necessary, to add thereto, a cross-bill, making the plaintiff and all defendants, whose interests were not identical with his, or who would not join with him in case their interests were identical, in a cross-bill, defendants to the same.

A petitioner's right to intervene is controlled by statute 41 providing that in an action either in law or in 

41a C. L. '29 (14019). 

41 As to rights of junior mortgagee, see 19 R. C. L. 530, and cases cited, and note in 36 L. R. A. (N. S.) 435.

260

[$equity, any one claiming an interest in the litigation may, at any time, be permitted to assert his right by intervention, but the intervention shall be in subordination to, and in recognition of, the propriety of the main proceeding. 

It has been held in Michigan that "a junior incumbrancer, becoming such after institution of proceedings to foreclose a prior mortgage lien, is not a necessary party defendant, and has no right to intervene in a foreclosure suit, regardless of statute, and that judicial policy is opposed to permitting intervention in such circumstances," the court saying, "a purchaser or incumbrancer pendente lite can always be protected in his interests in the property by filing his own original bill asserting his claim to the property. In this way a mortgagee is permitted to conduct his foreclosure proceeding in an orderly manner, and to proceed to a judicial determination of his rights as against his mortgagor and the mortgaged property," citing Steele v. Taylor, 1 Minn. 274, (Gil. 210).41b 

41b Union Trust Co. v. C. H. 

Miles Corp., 247 Mich. 340. 

Inasmuch as the decision in this case was based primarily upon the fact that the party proposing to intervene did not seek intervention in subordination to and in recognition of the propriety of the main proceeding as required by statute, and as the holding of the court with reference to the right of a junior incumbrancer becoming such after institution of proceedings to foreclose prior mortgage lien was not necessary to the decision of this case, in future litigation upon a like question this holding of the court may be looked upon as a mere dictum; and if a junior mortgagee can show that he has real interests to be protected, and petitions to intervene in subordination to and in recognition of the propriety of the main proceeding, quite likely the court might permit him to do so.

While it is true that a purchaser or incumbrancer, pendente lite, can always be protected in his interests in the property by filing his own original bill, asserting his claim to the property, circumstances might arise where full relief could not be obtained, by such independent suit, and if he should file his petition for intervention at an early stage of the proceedings so that there would be no delay in the main case it might be in the interest of justice to permit him to intervene. It certainly would avoid a multiplicity of suits, and while junior mortgagees are not necessary parties 261
