Questions of Priority. It has been held in some jurisdictions that a question of priority between mortgages may be settled in a foreclosure suit upon a first mortgage by allowing the second mortgagee to intervene and set up the statute of limitations or other defenses as a bar to the mortgage upon which the suit was brought; and in like manner judgment creditors have been allowed to intervene and contest the validity of a to a suit to foreclose a prior mortgage, if they have any interests that would be affected by the main suit and are not permitted to have a voice therein, they might be able to attack the proceedings for alleged fraud, or for any other reason that would appeal to the conscience of the court. 

Inasmuch as the Statute, C. L. '29 (14365), requires the plaintiff in his bill to state the names of all parties who have acquired interests derived from the mortgagor, since the giving of the mortgage, making them parties thereto, it seems absurd to say that parties acquiring an interest after the filing of the bill should under no circumstances be permitted to intervene in order to protect such interests as seem to be contemplated under this statute.

§ 391. Wife of Mortgagor. Where a mortgage is made by a husband alone upon his real estate the foreclosure thereof would not affect the right to dower in the property held by his wife, and she would not be an interested party in the foreclosure upon such estate, but in the case of a mortgage upon the homestead the wife would have an interest which she should be permitted to protect by intervention in case she was not made a party to the suit in the first instance.46

Where a mortgage was made by a single man who afterwards became married, his wife would have her dower rights in the land subject to the mortgage, and might have the right to redeem from a mortgage in order to protect such dower right.

The right of intervention depends to a large extent upon the right of redemption.

I. COMPLAINT OR BILL. 

§ 396. Where Filed. The Michigan Statute provides that all bills for the foreclosure or satisfaction of mortgages shall be filed in the circuit court in chancery of the county where the mortgaged premises or any part thereof are situated.' The primary purpose of a bill of complaint for the foreclosure of a mortgage is to show the grounds of the plaintiff's right, and to bring before the court all of the parties whose interests are sought to be foreclosed. If the bill does this, a decree for the plain- 

1 C. L. 29 (14364). See cases cited under C. L. '29 (13997). 266

[§ tiff follows in due course, providing he makes a sufficient case, and its effect is not limited nor the title made by sale thereunder impaired by any failure on the part of the plaintiff to state every right or interest of the defendants that is subject to the mortgage.2 

§ 397. Description of Property. The mortgaged prop erty must be described in the bill with sufficient accuracy, and in certain instances it must be described more accurately than in the mortgage itself. If the description in the mortgage is accurate, then it may be followed literally in the bill of complaint. But if it is not sufficiently definite, if copied into a bill to foreclose a mortgage, to render it good without additional averment, then such additional averment must be made to thoroughly identify the property. If, however, the description in the mortgage itself is so indefinite as to render it void, it follows as a matter of course that no allegations in a bill to foreclose the mortgage will avail. It may be that a description in the mortgage would be sufficient as to the parties to the mortgage to make it a binding obligation and yet, the mortgage might not sufficiently identify the property so that a deed could be based upon such description, and where the rights of other parties had intervened the record of the mortgage might not be sufficient to give them any notice of the interest of the mortgagee. In such case, the interests of such intervening parties could not be affected by any foreclosure proceeding. But where such interests have not intervened, the bill of complaint could properly describe the property intended to have been mortgaged, and if necessary, the mortgage itself might be reformed so as to embrace a proper description, in the same proceedings.

 § 398. Description of Note or Bond Secured. Where the note produced does not correspond with that described in the mortgage, either by reason of a misdescription in the mortgage or in consequence of renewal of the paper originally secured, the complaint ought to contain specific averments connecting the note sued on with the mortgage given. A mortgagee may enforce payment of the principal mortgage note and another given for interest in the same action, and a complaint to recover on a note and to foreclose a mortgage given to secure it does not state two separate causes of action. 

The plaintiff may be entitled to recover judgment on the note although the mortgage is void. The complaint in an action to foreclose a mortgage and to reform the certificate of acknowledgment of notary thereto states but one cause of action.¹ 

§ 399. Rents and Profits Pending Foreclosure. It has been held that one who seeks to enforce a mortgage lien against property which, through depreciation, has become worth less than the debt, may amend his complaint so as to claim the rents and profits of such property and such amendment does not add a new cause of action. 

Under the Michigan Statutes the mortgagor has the right to the use of the premises until his equity of redemption has been foreclosed, and this would be the case even if the mortgage were entirely inadequate to secure the debt. 

If the mortgagee, however, was committing any waste upon the premises so that when the equity of redemption has expired the value of the premises would be greatly depreciated by such waste, he could be restrained from waste. An action of this kind could be brought either before or after foreclosure proceedings were begun or an injunction could be asked in the foreclosure bill."

§ 400. Instalments on Principal or Interest, Taxes. 

Foreclosure may be brought for the failure to pay an instalment due upon the mortgage, or the failure to pay taxes upon the mortgaged property required by the mortgage to be paid by the mortgagor, or for the failure to pay the interest provided in the mortgage. If the mortgage provides that the mortgagee may, upon the failure to pay any instalment falling due or interest or taxes, declare the whole amount due and payable and, if it is desired by the mortgagee to foreclose for the whole amount, the bill of complaint should specifically set forth the fact that it is filed for that purpose, and should embrace an election to declare the whole amount payable unless an election has been theretofore made, and in that instance it should recite the fact that the election had been theretofore made." 

§ 401. Parties to Bill. The bill of complaint should make all persons defendants who own any interest in the property in question affected by the mortgage derived from the mortgagor, and just before filing the bill of complaint the attorney preparing the same should cause search to be made of the records in the register's office to see whether any interests have arisen in others than the mortgagor since the giving of the mortgage, and if he finds any such interests, the bill should contain a statement in relation thereto making such parties in interest defendants to the action for the foreclosure of the mortgage."

§ 402. Certain Statutory Provisions. Upon the filing of bill for the foreclosure or satisfaction of a mortgage, the plaintiff shall state therein whether any proceedings have been had at law for the recovery of the debt secured thereby or any part thereof, and whether any such debt or any part thereof has been collected or paid.¹¹ 

The bill of complaint shall set forth the names of all of the parties thereto, both plaintiff and defendant, and where different causes of action are set forth in a bill, such cause of action shall be stated in a separate division thereof and each of such divisions shall be complete in itself as near as may be and such divisions shall be numbered consecutively.12

The prayer of every bill of complaint shall be divided into paragraphs numbered consecutively and shall specify the particular relief which the plaintiff shall conceive himself entitled to, and may also contain a prayer for general relief.

II. ANSWER AND CROSS-BILL. 

§ 403. General Principles. The answer and cross-bill are in general subject to all of the provisions in reference to such pleadings in a court of chancery. The bill of complaint should be sworn to and unless answer under oath is waived, the answer should be sworn to by the defendant. "Where a bill shall be filed in chancery other than for discovery only, the plaintiff may waive the answer being made on the oath of the defendant, and in such case the answer may be made without oath and shall have no other or greater force than the bill." 14 

Michigan Circuit Court Rule No. 23 provides: "Section 1. Whenever in a cause a sworn bill of complaint is filed and a sworn answer demanded, the defendant shall be required to file such sworn answer. But neither a sworn bill nor a sworn answer shall have the force of evidence except as to admissions and except on the hearing of motions and petitions. "Section 2. Every answer shall contain an explicit admission or denial of each allegation in the bill of complaint as to which the defendant has knowledge or belief. 

But as to matters charged in the bill as to which the defendant avers he has no knowledge sufficient to form a belief, he shall not be required to admit nor deny the same, but shall state his want of such knowledge. And

18 C. L. '29 (14400). 271

every material allegation in the bill to which the defendant shall not make answer shall be taken as admitted by the defendant. "Section 3. Pleas in equitable actions, other than pleas in abatement and to the jurisdiction (which are abolished by statute) are abolished, and all defenses which might formerly be raised by such pleas shall be interposed by answer, provided, that on cause shown by motion an issue so raised may be heard in advance of the trial in the cause. "If cross-bill is filed when there are other cross defendants besides the plaintiff in the case, a chancery summons should be issued and served upon them.” § 404. Parties to Cross-Bill. Stated in a general way, the defendant has the right to deny any of the allegations contained in the plaintiff's bill of complaint. The defendant may set up the fact that his claim is a prior lien to that of the plaintiff without filing a cross-bill. If the court finds that his lien is a prior lien in the decree in favor of the plaintiff as against other parties it may provide for the payment of such prior lien. However, the party claiming a prior lien may, if he chooses so to do, answer the general allegations of the bill in the usual manner and set up the fact of his claimed prior lien in a cross-bill and pray for a foreclosure of the same in case there has been a forfeiture under the terms of his prior lien, in which case all parties interested should be made defendants to the said cross-bill, and if necessary new parties should be brought into the case in order that a just hearing might be had upon such cross-bill. What has been said with reference to bringing in new parties in a cross-bill under the particular circumstances cited would apply to all cases where the defendants should find it necessary to file a cross-bill and when other parties than those made parties to the original bill would be interested in the matters set up in the cross-bill. 

It has been held that where a junior mortgagee made party defendant to a suit for foreclosure of a prior mort- 272

[§ gage seeks relief upon a cross-bill against a sale made by the prior mortgagor pendente lite under a power of sale in his mortgage the purchaser at the sale is an indispensable party to the cross-bill.15 

§ 405. Defenses and Set-off. In general, obviously, defenses going to the validity of a mortgage may be asserted in a suit seeking its foreclosure, though it is to be noted generally that no other or further defenses are allowed in an action to foreclose a mortgage given to secure a negotiable instrument, than would be allowed in an action on such negotiable instrument.16 No defense can be set up against suit by an assignee that was not available at the time of the assignment.17 

§ 406. Statute of Limitations. Broadly speaking, one who may defend against the foreclosure of a mortgage lien may object that before the action was commenced against him the lien had expired, or that the statute of limitations had run. In like manner, one who, either by private or judicial sale, has become the owner of interests in real estate belonging to one or more heirs at law of a mortgagor may plead the statute in bar of an action to foreclose the mortgage on the real estate so acquired although each and all of such heirs at law are parties to the action and neglect or refuse to interpose the plea.17

$407. Defenses and Set-off Available Against Pur chase Money Mortgage. Where a proceeding is brought to foreclose a purchase money mortgage the defendant may, of course, set up defenses going to the validity of the mortgage. It is well settled, however, that a purchaser of land who has gone into possession and accepted a deed cannot, in the absence of fraud or mistake and in the absence of eviction or something equivalent thereto set up a failure or defect of title as a defense to the foreclosure of a mortgage given for the purchase money. 

He must resort to his covenants, but the purchaser of land under a deed containing covenants against encumbrances, if he subsequently pays off and discharges any encumbrances, may set off the amount which he has paid against the amount due on a mortgage for the purchase price, or he may give notice to his vendor requiring him to pay off the encumbrance. It has also been held that in an action to foreclose a purchase money mortgage, the mortgagor may claim a reduction of the mortgage debt if the quantity of land covered by the mortgage has been fraudulently represented to be greater than that actually conveyed and such representations have induced the purchase, unless he has elected to pursue another remedy by bringing an action to reform the deed, in which a reformation of the deed so as to include all of the land so purchased has been decreed.19

§ 408. Fraud in the Procuring of the Instrument. 

Where fraud in procuring the instrument is established an assignee seeking to foreclose the same must establish by the preponderance of evidence that he was the holder for value before due without notice.20

While contracts between agents of a corporation occupying positions of trust and confidence and a corporation fairly entered into and honestly executed, where no one is defrauded or overreached, are not necessarily invalid, such contracts will always be scrutinized with jealous care by courts to see that no advantage is taken of the corporation or the rights and interests of its stockholders jeopardized.

Officers of a corporation may deal with it in good faith if their acts are fair, open and known to the directors and stockholders; such contracts are not absolutely void, but they are voidable at the election of the party whose interest has been so represented.

If a third person join with a corporate officer in dealing with the corporation, with knowledge that he is such officer, the contract may be set aside as to him as well as the corporate officer upon the theory that where a stranger participates with such officer such corporation in the commission of an act of manifest bad faith or breach of duty to it, he, equally with the officer, commits a wrong and ought not to derive profit from it.20a

Where a seller showed to a buyer valuable lake frontage and represented to him that he was acquiring the same, when in fact the land conveyed was other land of much less value, the buyer is entitled to recover his damages for the fraud whether the seller intended to defraud him or not.20b

Where fraud is alleged as a ground upon which a rehearing is sought after the expiration of the period in

III. ANSWER TO CROSS-BILL. 

§ 409. Necessity for Answer. If a cross-bill is filed, the plaintiff and other cross-defendants, if any, should file an answer to the cross-bill. In Michigan, under the 

Judicature Act a replication is not required to the defendant's answer but the case is deemed at issue when all parties made defendant have answered the plaintiff's bill of complaint and if cross-bills have been filed when cross-defendants have filed their answers to such crossbills. As in an ordinary chancery proceeding, the case will not go to hearing until it is at issue as to all parties named as defendants in the bill of complaint, unless the default has been taken of such parties as have not appeared and such parties as have appeared and have not answered. It may be necessary, as in other cases where it is impossible to get personal service, to get substituted service by publication or, in certain instances, to dismiss the bill as to parties against whom service has not been had.21

 I. IN GENERAL. 

§ 410. Certain Statutory Provisions. Some other pro visions of the Statutes of the State of Michigan with reference to the foreclosure of mortgages are as follows:

A sale shall not be ordered to be made within six months after the filing of the bill of foreclosure, and it is also provided that the mortgagor, his heirs, executors, administrators, or any person lawfully claiming from or under any of them shall, within six months from the time of such sale, have the right to redeem therefrom in the manner provided by the said section.¹ 

In the original decree the court shall determine and decree as to which defendants, if any, are personally liable for the mortgage debt, and it shall be provided in the decree that upon the coming in and the confirmation of the commissioner's report of sale, if there be any part of the money decreed to be due, either the principal or interest of the debt or the costs decreed to be paid, left unpaid after applying the amount received by the commissioner upon the sale of the premises, the clerk shall, upon the application of the attorney for the plaintiff and without notice to the defendant or his attorney, issue execution for the amount of such deficiency.2

If a bill shall be filed, while the same is pending and after a decree shall be rendered thereon, no proceedings whatever shall be had at law for the recovery of the debt secured by the mortgage or any part thereof unless authorized by the court.

All sales of mortgaged premises under a decree in chancery shall be made by a circuit court commissioner of the county in which the decree was rendered or the land or some part thereof situated, or by some other person duly authorized by the order of the court.  II. EVIDENCE. 

§ 411. Parol Evidence. An attorney who drafts a mortgage and signs it as a witness is entitled to testify as to what occurred at the time of its execution. A mortgage expressed to secure a stipulated obligation may be shown to have been given to secure one entirely different and distinct, this doctrine resting on the familiar rule that parol evidence is admissible to apply a written contract to its subject matter. So if a mortgage is given to secure a note, and it is provided in the instrument that the payee agrees to renew it from time to time, evidence is admissible to show that a note bearing a later date is a renewal of that first given.10 

§ 412. Necessity for Production of Mortgage Notes- 

Evidence of Indebtedness. It has been held that if the execution and genuineness of notes secured by mortgage sought to be foreclosed are denied, the recital of their execution and delivery in the mortgage is alone insufficient after the maturity of the notes to prove the existence of the indebtedness secured by the mortgage, and that in the absence of the production of such notes by the person claiming under them, they will be presumed to have been paid. It has also been held that it is error to receive the mortgage in evidence, without first producing or accounting for the note which it secured. And if a bond secured by mortgage is not produced or its loss accounted for, the presumption of payment of the mortgage debt is conclusive. On the other hand, according to some decisions, if a mortgage or trust deed recites indebtedness, nonpayment thereof is presumed and that presumption can only be rebutted by affirmative proof of payment. While there are decisions to the contrary, it seems that where a mortgage, in distinct terms, states the existence of indebtedness from the mortgagor to the

876, 53 S. E. 699, 110 Am. St. Rep. 207. 280

When the consideration expressed in a mortgage is in dispute, parol evidence is admissible to show the real consideration, but when the consideration is not in dispute parol evidence is not admissible to change the terms of the mortgage in regard to the payment of notes described therein. And the written contract, as evidenced by the bonds and mortgage, cannot be varied, in the absence of fraud, accident, or mistake, in a suit to foreclose the mortgage by evidence of a parol agreement to the effect

III. DECREE. 

§ 416. Absent Defendant-Infant. No personal de cree can be taken against an absent defendant brought in by publication and not appearing, nor against an infant without proofs. The effect of a default in a suit to foreclose for an instalment is only to admit the securities as alleged and the amount then due, and cannot operate as an admission of the nonpayment of an instalment not yet due.22 It is the practice in this state on foreclosures to allow a reasonable time for payment definitely fixed by the decree.28

Mortgagee is entitled to pay defaulted taxes and have amount thereof included in decree in foreclosure although mortgage does not so provide.23 However, if one who purchases the property at the foreclosure sale thereafter pays delinquent taxes, he cannot insist upon repayment in order to make redemption complete, as the statute fixes the terms upon which redemption may be had. 

§417. Principles Governing the Distribution of As sets. Some of the most difficult questions arising under the whole subject of mortgages relate to the distribution of assets realized from the sale of mortgaged property, and to the form of decrees, where several properties are covered by the same mortgage, and where subsequent conveyances have been made of portions of such property, either in the form of mortgages or deeds, or where liens of any nature have been created thereon subsequent to such mortgage. If several principles are continually borne in mind in the consideration of these questions, it will be found that many supposed difficulties will vanish.

§ 423. Deficiency. The decree of the court authorizes the sale of the mortgaged premises and determines as to which defendants, if any, are personally liable for the mortgage debt and provides further that upon the coming in and confirmation of the commissioners' report of sale, if there be any part of the money decreed to be due, either the principal or interest of the debt or the costs decreed to be paid, left unpaid after applying the amount received by the commissioners upon the sale of the premises, the clerk of the court shall, upon the application by the attorney for the plaintiff and without notice to the defendant or his attorney, issue execution for the amount of such deficiency.5 This section is a modification of the law as it existed prior to the adoption of the Judicature Act. It will be observed that the law as it now stands provides for the hearing of all questions in the original case and the fixing by final decree before sale of the status of all of the parties to the case. Any matters arising thereafter are nonjudicial questions but relate simply to the duties of ministerial or clerical officers. 

Under the law as it formerly stood, a decree was made for the sale of the mortgaged premises, and on the coming in of the report of sale, it was provided that the court should have power to decree the payment by the mortgagor of any balance of the mortgage debt that might remain unsatisfied after a sale of the mortgaged premises in the cases in which such balance is recoverable at law, and for that purpose that the court might issue the necessary execution as in other cases as against other property of the mortgagor.46

By another section of the law as it formerly existed " it was provided that if the mortgage debt be secured by

One may limit his responsibility, by the promissory note given with the mortgage, to the proceeds of the land only. 48a

It is not sufficient that one should take a deed to property mortgaged, containing a provision that it is made subject to a certain mortgage, but in order that the grantee should be charged with the payment thereof the deed must contain the words that the grantee assumes the mortgage and agrees to pay it. This obligation cannot be enforced by the mortgagee against the grantee in a suit at law, but can only be enforced by such mortgagee in chancery proceedings brought for that purpose, as for instance the foreclosure of the mortgage in question.48b 

It was held in an early case that a guaranty of collection of a debt secured by mortgage creates no obligation on the part of the guarantor to pay until after foreclosure decree and a failure to obtain payment out of the mortgaged premises and out of other property of the principal; and such guarantor ought not to be made a party defendant to the foreclosure suit.48c

[§ 424a deficiency on foreclosure is new and supplementary and not a mere continuation of the foreclosure; 50 and that there must be a special application for the issue of an execution, if that is desired, and notice of the application for the issue of an execution, given to the defendant."1

It was contemplated that the defendant be brought in on petition and notice. If he contested the right to an execution, he would be required to file his answer setting out the grounds of his objection, these grounds not to be inconsistent with the decree but usually such as operates in its discharge. In such proceedings, the validity or justice of the decree could not be inquired into. It was required that the answer should be under oath, and the complainant could take issue on it, and a reference might be ordered to take proof, the burden in such case being upon the defendant.52

It was held that no objections could be made to the issuing of an execution for a deficiency unless it arose after confirmation of the foreclosure sale and recognized the decree and went to its discharge.58 

The statute of limitations begins to run against the right of a mortgagee to an execution for a deficiency from the entry of the decree of foreclosure, although the liability of the mortgagor cannot be enforced until the sale is made, and the report thereof is filed fixing the amount of such deficiency.58

This constitutes the enrollment of the decree.57

V. RAILROAD MORTGAGES AND FORECLOSURE THEREOF. 

§ 429. Rights of Citizens and Others Interested. In cases involving a railroad mortgage foreclosure it was held that citizens and others interested were entitled to purchase the property in its entirety for continuance as a common carrier, even though the railroad had been running at a loss, and that a decree requiring property standing in the name of an independent corporation, which was in practical effect a subsidiary or instrumentality of the railroad for getting business, and was with the property of the railroad, mortgaged as an entirety before the incorporation of the two companies, to be sold as part of the assets of the railroad was proper. 

The appointment of a receiver to take charge and conserve the property of the railroad which had been running at a loss was proper, but that the absolute absorption of the limited assets of a small branch railroad which had been running at a loss or their incumbrance by receiver's certificates issued to repair equipment for operation, and operate the line on the speculative hazard of the receiver being able to secure business sufficient to put it on a sustaining basis and facilitate a possible sale, was improper.76

VI. ANCILLARY PROCEEDINGS. 

§ 432. Rental Subsequent to Expiration of Equity of 

Redemption. Under C. L. '15 (12675–12692), C. L. '29 (14364-14380), providing for the foreclosure of mortgages, no provision is made for proceedings subsequent to a valid decree, sale, confirmation, and expiration of the period of redemption, except to put the purchaser in possession of the premises, and therefore the court has no jurisdiction, in foreclosure suits, to determine liability for rents collected by the mortgagor's trustee, after expiration of the redemption period.81 

§ 432a. Collateral Attack of the Validity of Proceed ings. The validity of foreclosure proceedings from which no appeal was taken may not be assailed by mortgagor, who had lost all interest in the property, on petition to open decree foreclosing another mortgage, to have the sale set aside and a rehearing granted. It was subsequently held that one who had lost all interest in property by foreclosure of another mortgage, and who was made party to present foreclosure proceedings for the purpose of securing deficiency decree against her had no interest affected by decree therein which made no provision for deficiency.

I. IN GENERAL. 

§ 433. Tendency Toward Unification in Foreclosure 

Cases. Inasmuch as the courts in recent years have had a tendency in chancery proceedings involving the foreclosing of land contracts toward the unification of the practice in such cases and in the foreclosing of real estate mortgages, it has been suggested that a chapter in this book be devoted to the subject of the foreclosure of land contracts by chancery proceedings.

There will be no attempt to treat exhaustively the law of land contracts, but a few general principles in relation to land contracts will be mentioned as a necessary premise to the discussion of the particular question involved. 

§ 434. Distinguished from Mere Option. A land con tract should be distinguished from a mere option, where the person considering the purchase of land acquires the right within a certain time to make such purchase. 

He does not obligate himself to make any payments beyond those by which the option is secured. He can refuse to take the property if he desires to do so. The only litigation likely to result from that kind of an agreement is as to the questions of the acceptance of the option by the optionee, the adequacy of consideration for the option, and the violation of the terms of the option by the grantor thereof. An option to purchase land does not, before acceptance, convey to the holder any interest in the premises. A purchaser of land under an oral agreement, who goes into possession thereof and 304

[§ 

makes improvements, may not invoke the doctrine of part performance under C. L. '15 (11979); C. L. '29 (13415).¹ 

§ 435. Distinguished from Mortgage. The question sometimes arises as to whether the interests of the parties are governed by the law of vendor and vendee, or the law of mortgages. Where the transaction is merely one of loaning money and giving security therefor the relation created is that of mortgagor and mortgagee, notwithstanding the transaction is evidenced by giving a deed and taking back a land contract. 

§ 436. Contract May Arise from Correspondence. The rule, requiring a contract for the purchase of land to be in writing, is satisfied by a written offer to sell on deferred payment plan, made in the form of a letter, which is accepted by telegram before the same is withdrawn, and it may be specifically enforced.

The offer in such instance must be sufficiently definite upon all essential points to form a contract when accepted, and the acceptance must be unequivocal, without the attempt to inject any new offer into the transaction.

II. TITLE TO PROPERTY UNDER CONTRACT. 

§ 437. Interests of the Respective Parties. A con tract for the sale of land conveys to the vendee an equitable title, and the only principle upon which the vendor may sue for his money, and at the same time seek security against the land, is that which recognizes the analogy to the vendor's lien in cases where the legal title has been conveyed, and the vendee's title can only be divested by a sale. In land contracts, as in mortgages, 1 Windiate v. Leland, 246 Mich. 659. 

2 Reid v. Dowd, 257 Mich. 492; 

Denby v. Ozeran, 255 Mich. 477; 

Rowe v. Wm. Ford & Co., 257 Mich. 646. 

3 Quinn v. Feaheny, 252 Mich. 526. 305

§ 437] 

there is no such thing as a strict foreclosure of such a lien.4

A vendee's interest under an executory contract is an equitable title in the land, while the vendor holds the legal title." 

Where one purchases property under a land contract and enters into possession of the same, using and occupying it as a home he is equitably and in fact the owner, although the contract is in the names of others who advanced for him the down payment thereon. 

It has been held that the interest which the vendee has in a land contract is real property, and that he is the equitable owner thereof," while that of the vendor is personal property.

While not criticizing the decisions that hold that the vendor is the trustee for the purchaser, and that his interest is a mere chattel interest, one should be cautioned against emphasizing these particular conclusions in relation to the law of vendor and vendee; the interests of these parties are governed by the law of real property, and particularly by the law as it has developed with reference to those contracts which relate to the sale of real property.

The law of trusts and the law in relation to chattel property has each its own field, and it is likely that more confusion than clarity will be gained by treating land contracts which are clear in their expression, as creating some relation which does not exist under the specific

terms of such contracts. People enter into executory land contracts because they desire to accomplish certain ends which they could not well accomplish in any other way, and to treat such an agreement as though it were an agreement for some other purpose, or to relegate it to a class of agreements to which its authors never intended it should belong, might deprive parties desiring to operate in a certain way of carrying out their arrangements according to their intentions, and close that particular field of operations from a use to which it might legitimately be put.

The positions of the vendor and vendee may change very radically while carrying out the terms of a land contract. When they enter upon their relations it is quite possible that the vendor may intend to retain the title to the land, and such control thereof as is legally possible until the vendee has paid such a substantial amount thereon as to give to him a valuable equity, and yet the down payment may be a very trifling amount in comparison to the value of the property. According to the intention of the parties, if the vendee should find it impossible to follow up a small payment with such other payments as are required under the terms of the contract, the vendor might, without offending against ideas of equity and justice, retake the property with no more ceremony than a landlord would use in retaking property to which he had given a lease. To say in this early state of the relations that the grantor had only a chattel title, and that he is trustee for the grantee, and that the grantee is trustee for certain funds for the grantor,10 while it might have within it an element of truth, it would be carrying certain principles to an extent that would make them ludicrous. The grantee, with no funds in his hands, and only a hope that he might become able to pay for the land to which he has a contract upon which he has made only a negligible payment, 10 House v. Dexter, 9 Mich. 246;

Wing v. McDowell, Walk. Ch. 

(Mich:) 175. 307

§ 437] 

can only by a stretch of the imagination be said to be a trustee of certain large funds of money which he may never acquire, and which he expects, if he does acquire, he will pay upon such land contract. 

In Detroit and Security Trust Co. v. Kramer, 247 Mich. 

468, the court discusses at considerable length the extent to which some of the earlier holdings of the court may lead to confusion. The court in that case said: "The holdings of courts that upon the execution and delivery of such a contract, the remaining interest of the vendor in the property becomes personalty and the interest of the vendee realty, are based upon the theory of equitable conversion. It is said the vendor holds the title to the land in trust for the vendee, and likewise the vendee holds the purchase price in trust for the vendor. 

As has been pointed out by eminent authority, this theory at best is somewhat far fetched. See note to

Pomeroy Equity Jurisprudence (4th Ed.), sec. 2261. 

Necessity has compelled the adoption of some rule of property by which the rights of descent and distribution are definitely fixed; and it may be conceded that in the absence of some controlling circumstances to the contrary, the application of the doctrine of equitable conversion in the manner above suggested accomplishes a fairly just result. But this theory, which is no more than a legal fiction, should not be applied in such a manner or under such circumstances as will confessedly defeat the disposition that one may make of his or her property, so long as such disposition is not in violation of law. "Carried to its logical conclusion, the doctrine of equitable conversion leads to many strange and serious results, especially as applied to lands held by the entireties."

In this case the grantors were husband and wife, and the question of the right of survivorship arose. The court further said: "Regardless of what may have been said in some of the earlier decisions of this court, it is now the established law of this state that in the absence of statutory provisions to the contrary a right of sur- 308

[§ vivorship may be created in personal property." (Citing cases.) "We think it conclusively appears in this record that Mr. and Mrs. Kramer so arranged their respective properties that in effect it amounted to a contractual undertaking that each should take and hold a right of survivorship in the other's property." And the court held that under the circumstances of that case the vendors held their interests as tenants by the entireties, and that the survivor was entitled to all of the interests of the vendors under the contract. 

In Moore v. Van Goosen, 250 Mich. 67, where husband and wife sold properties which they had owned by the entireties on land contracts in which, as vendors, they were described as tenants by the entireties, and in exchange took other lots as tenants by the entireties, the court held that there was nothing to indicate that the funds, entirety property at their inception, lost their character before being reinvested in the entirety property in question. 

Under a recent statute 11 where husband and wife are the vendors of real property upon land contract providing for future payments to be made to them, they would hold by the entireties.

Where the vendor has made nearly all of the payments necessary to entitle him to a deed to the property in question, and the vendor's interest in the lands has been correspondingly reduced to a trifling amount, then the principles that have been evolved during the course of years in the treatment of the relations of vendor and vendee by which the vendor's interests are carefully guarded, are found to be most reasonable. Usually the relations of these parties never reach the point where it would offer good security for the balance, he is permitted to take a deed to the property and give a mortgage back for what remains unpaid.

 III. REMEDIES OF VENDOR IN CASE OF DELINQUENCY UPON PART OF VENDEE. 

§ 438. Taking Possession Without Legal Process. It has sometimes been said that inasmuch as proceedings brought before a circuit court commissioner were merely for the purpose of testing the right of possession, and that they do not go to the extent of testing the title of the property,12 the vendor having the right to repossess himself of the premises upon failure of the vendee to make his payments, if he can gain peaceful possession of the premises, may simply enter upon the same and declare the contract forfeited, without any legal procedure. 

That method might be effective where property was in such condition as not to be capable of visible possession on the part of the vendee or in case of abandoned property, upon which buildings had been constructed. 

It has been held that while forfeiture may be contracted for as a basis for expeditious determination of the relation of the vendor and vendee in a land contract, drastic measures taken after forfeiture to seize possession without warning and thereby cut off the vendee's last chance to redeem, as recognized in summary proceedings, are not between vendor and vendee entitled in equity to as tolerant consideration as in cases involving only the relation of landlord and tenant.¹ 18

§ 443. Equity Will Not Enforce Forfeitures. Equity will not enforce a nonassignable clause in a land contract. 

In a recent Michigan case, where vendors asked the court in chancery to cancel a contract because of an assignment contrary to its terms, the court said: "If it could be said that for this reason they might have such a right, in any case, they have none in this, because the contract does not give it to them. It declares some causes of forfeiture, but does not include a violation of the non-assignability clause. None can be implied. In view of these facts, if the vendors have any remedy because of the assignment, it is an action for damages for breach of the covenant. They are not entitled to declare a forfeiture, and, if they were, this court could not aid them. Equity dislikes forfeitures and not only will not aid in enforcing them, but will restrict their effect as far as possible." 17

In considering matters as to the failure to enforce strict performance of a land contract the question as to .whether time is made of the essence of the contract is sometimes controlling. Where time is made of the essence of the contract failure to pay at the appointed time justifies immediate forfeiture.28 But equity does not favor forfeitures, and when time is not of the essence of the contract, relieves against them.29 When harsh and hasty steps to enforce for default in payment are unjust and inequitable, as where the vendee's default was acquiesced in or condoned over a long series of years, by a continued acceptance of payments by the vendors, time was not of the essence of the contract.30

And it has been held that where the vendor in a land contract, whether time is or is not of the essence thereof, repeatedly accepts past due payments, it is but equitable, in case he later seeks to rely upon a forfeiture provision of the contract, to require him to give notice of the amount due and of his intention to declare a forfeiture if the same is not paid within a stated time.³¹ 

§ 452. Acceleration of Payment Clause. A clause in a land contract to the effect that upon the failure of the purchaser to perform its conditions, the vendor may declare the whole amount due, is not illegal, but if this right is exercised immediately upon the happening of a minor default, the court of chancery will not enforce it.88

§ 458. Competency of Parties to Contract. In a case brought upon a contract for the purchase of land executed by husband and wife, while the husband was mentally incompetent, the court held that the same was unenforceable as to him, and that it could not be enforced against the wife, since she acquired no interest in the land separate and apart from that of her husband, but that the estate to be created by performance on the part of the vendor was one by the entireties.12 

VII. PLEADINGS. 

§ 459. General Rules of Equity Pleadings Apply. 

There is nothing peculiar to the pleadings in a land contract foreclosure case. One familiar with pleadings in ordinary chancery cases, and particularly in mortgage foreclosure cases, would need no suggestions with reference to pleadings and methods of procedure in a case involving the foreclosure of either the vendor's or vendee's lien in a land contract case. 

§ 460. Defendant May File a Cross-Bill. Without reference to the question as to which party may begin proceedings in a court of chancery for the preservation or enforcement of his rights under a land contract, if the other party believes he has interests that cannot be sufficiently protected by an answer, he could file a crossbill and procure such affirmative relief as he would be entitled to receive under the conditions arising. 

The liberality permitted in amendments in ordinary cases is exercised in favor of the parties to cases of this nature. A vendor's cross-bill asking only to reform the contract may be amended to ask for the amount due thereon, and for foreclosure.48

§ 461] 

 VIII. DECREE AND SUBSEQUENT PROCEEDINGS. 

§ 461. Right to Decree for Total Unpaid Purchase 

Price. Where there is no provision in a land contract permitting vendor to declare the whole purchase price due upon the default of vendee in any of its conditions, it would be error for the court to order a sale of the premises to satisfy the entire purchase price, both due and to become due since to do so would be to declare a forfeiture, which a court of equity will not do.44 

§ 462. Decree for Deficiency Against Assignee of 

Vendee. The doctrine that the court will have authority to grant a deficiency decree against an assignee of the vendee in a land contract who has assumed the contract and agreed to pay amounts falling due after assignment, is new to the State of Michigan. It has usually been held that the liability of a grantee in a deed to land subject to a mortgage, which he has assumed and agreed to pay, to a personal decree upon foreclosure of such mortgage, rests not upon any contractual relations alone between him and his grantor, but upon the statute providing that upon foreclosure a decree might be taken by the mortgagee against any person who is under obligation to pay the mortgage. Inasmuch as that statute does not apply to land contracts it has been believed that it is no authority for holding an assignee of a land contract to be liable under a decree for deficiency upon the foreclosure of such land contract.44a 

But in Lowrie & Robinson Lumber Co. v. Rubin, 245

Mich. 224, under the peculiar circumstances of that case, the court held that the assignee of the vendee of the land contract in question would be liable for a deficiency, if any occurred, after sale of the premises under foreclosure, and this decision has been followed in numerous instances from that time. 

44 Brown v. Mudge, 242 Mich. 324. 

448 Sheldon v. Erskine, 78 Mich. 

627; Peoples Sav. Bank v. Geistert, 253 Mich. 694, and cases cited. 322

[§ In Barnard v. Huff, 252 Mich. 258, the court discusses this question at great length, and gives the reasons for its conclusion, independent of any statutory provisions, that a deficiency decree might be entered against the assignee of a vendee of a land contract, who had assumed and agreed to pay the obligations of the vendee. Without quoting at length from the decision, the ultimate conclusion arrived at is stated in the following language: "As between the assignor and the assignee the latter becomes the principal debtor, and the former a surety, and the principles of subrogation apply. To this may be added the equitable doctrine of avoidance of multiplicity of suits and the province of equity to afford full relief and protect all rights. The deficiency decree properly ran against the vendee's assignee." (Citations omitted.) "An assignment of a land contract is a conveyance of vendee's equitable title. By analogy to the law of mortgages, the assignment binds the accepting assignee in equity without his signature to it.' 99 This remedy, however, is a purely equitable remedy, and the vendor may not maintain an action at law against the vendee's assignee for payments due under the contract, although the assignee agreed with vendee to perform the contract. In order for the vendor to have any legal right as against such assignee to payments there must be a novation of the account.45

The privity of obligation between a vendor and vendee in a land contract would not carry over to the assignee of vendee by naked quitclaim deed nor would a liability for deficiency arise under such transaction.46

Where there is no claim of fraud, one accepting an assignment of a land contract from the vendee cannot urge as a defense in a suit for foreclosure, with prayer for deficiency, that amounts stated in contract were fictitious and did not represent the actual sale of lots.

§ 463] 

On foreclosure of a land contract, vendor's rights, if any, against the contract purchaser from vendee depends upon terms of contract between vendee and his purchaser. There is no analogy between acceptance of deed subject to a mortgage, which grantee assumes and agrees to pay and land contract executed by vendee on sale by him to purchaser, with right of purchaser to pay instalments due on his vendor's contract; such leave to pay not being assumption of prior contract nor equitable assignment thereof with promise to pay the same."8 

In land contract foreclosure cases, as in mortgage foreclosures, the decree at the hearing may provide for execution for deficiency after sale, and no subsequent decree is necessary after the coming in of the report of the commissioner showing such deficiency. 49 

§ 463. Sale in Inverse Order of Alienation. The de cree may also be made to protect the interests of all parties before the court where there are conflicting interests represented in the foreclosure proceedings. It may provide for sale of property which has been resold in the inverse order of alienation, and may contain a provision to preserve rights of parties under a release clause contained in the contract. However, the assignee of the vendee is not entitled to the benefit of a provision in a contract for release of lots by vendor on payment of additional sums, where vendor was in default in contract payments; and in a suit to foreclose land contract against lots under contract of sale by vendee, but not released by vendor because of vendee's default, and where title for that reason had not passed, the rule requiring sale in inverse order of alienation is not applicable.50 

§ 464. Redemption After Decree. Circuit Rule No. 50, sec. 5, providing that sales under decrees of foreclosure 

50 McClure v. Meyer Corp., 254 

Mich. 686. 

48 Henning v. Levin, 259 Mich. 250. 

49 Grimore v. Beauch, 247 Mich. 439. 324

[§ 

shall not be ordered within six months after commencement of suit provides a practice to be followed in the foreclosure of mortgages, but has no application to land contracts.51

There being no statutory right to redeem from foreclosure of land contracts, time allowed in which to redeem is not a matter of right, but is entirely within the discretion of the court, procedure authorized by statute in the foreclosure of mortgages having no application to a land contract.52

In a case heard in the supreme court, in which a decree of the lower court was affirmed for the foreclosure of a land contract, where the period limited for redemption in the decree had long since expired before the making of the order confirming the same, the supreme court allowed an extension of thirty days from the filing of its opinion in which redemption might be had, after which order was made for the sale, as provided for in the decree of the lower court.58

No. 20. Clause Conferring Upon the Holder of a Debt of a Corporation the Right to Convert the Principal 

Thereof Into Stock of Such Corporation. 

And the directors of the said corporation having been duly authorized by the consent of two-thirds of the stockholders thereof, and having voted at a meeting duly and legally called for that purpose, to confer upon the holders of this and like obligations the right to convert the principal thereof after two and not more than twelve years from the date thereof into the stock of the said corporation; the holder of this instrument shall have the right at any time after two and not more than twelve years from its date to convert the principal thereof into the capital stock of the said corporation of the par value of the amount of such principal.

In all cases in which less than the entire amount of bonds are to be redeemed, the published notice of redemption shall contain the numbers of the bonds so to be redeemed. In all cases of redemption of bonds, the company shall, on or before the date fixed for redemption, deposit with the trustee sufficient money to pay the redemption price of said bonds and accrued interest to the date of redemption.

Section 2. The company owns and is lawfully possessed of all the trust estate by absolute title in fee simple, and the same is free and clear of all liens and incumbrances, and the company has full corporate power to exercise and is lawfully entitled to exercise all rights of ownership thereof and of every part thereof, and the company will warrant and defend the title of the trust estate and every part thereof to the trustee, and its successors and assigns, for the benefit of the holders for the time being of the bonds against the lawful claims and demands of all persons whatsoever. Article IV. 

Remedies of Trustee and Bondholders. 

Section 1. In case one or more of the following events, herein termed "events of default," shall happen, that is to say: (a) Default shall be made in payment of the principal or of any interest on any bond and any such default shall have continued for a period of thirty (30) days; (b) Default shall be made in the observance or performance of any of the other covenants or agreements of the company contained in this indenture, and any such default shall have continued for a period of sixty (60) days after written notice to the company from the trustee specifying such default and requiring the same to be remedied; (c) An order shall be made for the appointment of a receiver or receivers of the company, or any substantial part of its property; (d) The company shall bè adjudicated a bankrupt; (e) The company shall make an assignment for the benefit of its creditors or shall admit in writing its inability to pay its debts, or corporate action shall be taken by it in furtherance of either of the aforesaid purposes, or to procure a receivership for its property; (f) Any judgment or decree for a sum of money shall be entered against the company, and such judgment or decree shall remain for thirty (30) days unsatisfied and unsecured unless appeal is duly prosecuted therefrom with stay of execution or enforcement thereof; then and in every such case the trustee may, and upon 518

FORMS 

[No. 76 the request of the holders of a majority in interest of the bonds hereby secured and then outstanding, and being first indemnified by them to its satisfaction, shall proceed forthwith to enforce the rights of said trustee and of the bondholders hereunder, by sale or entry, or both, according to such requisition, or by judicial proceedings for such purpose as the trustee, being advised by counsel, shall deem most expedient in the interest of holders of the bonds secured hereby. If the trustee shall proceed by sale then the trustee shall, with or without entry, sell all the premises, estate, property and rights hereby conveyed, or so intended to be, at public auction or vendue, and upon such sale make, execute and deliver to the purchaser or purchasers, his or their heirs or assigns, forever, a good and sufficient conveyance at law, which sale shall be a perpetual bar, both in law and in equity, against the said company and all persons or incorporators lawfully claiming or to claim by, to or under it, and upon the making of any such sale the principal of all the bonds hereby secured and then outstanding shall forthwith become due and payable, anything in said bonds to the contrary notwithstanding. In any and all cases a notice of sale shall be given as required by the Statutes of the state of Michigan, in such case made and provided. 

Section 2. Upon the making of any sale, whether under the power of sale hereby granted, or pursuant to judicial proceedings, the said trustee shall apply the proceeds to such sale as follows: (1) To the payment of the cost and expenses of such sale or sales, including a reasonable compensation to said trustee, its agents, attorneys and counsel, and all expenses, liabilities and advances made and incurred by said trustee in managing and maintaining the property hereby conveyed or intended to be, and all taxes, assessments, charges or liens superior to the lien of these presents. (2) To the payment of the whole amount of principal and interest which shall then be owing or unpaid upon 519

No. 76]  

the bonds secured hereby, without preference or priority whatever, whether the said principal, by the tenor of said bonds, be then due or yet to become due, and in case of the insufficiency of such proceeds to pay in full the whole amount of such principal and interest owing and unpaid upon the said bonds, then to the payment of such principal and interest, pro rata, without preference or priority, but ratably, to the aggregate amount of such principal and accrued and unpaid interest. (3) To pay over the surplus, if any, to whomsoever may be lawfully entitled to receive the same. 

Section 3. In case of any sale hereunder, any purchaser, for the purpose of making settlement or payment for the property purchased, shall be entitled to turn in any bonds and any matured and unpaid coupons appertaining thereto, in order that there may be credited as paid thereon the sums payable out of the net proceeds of such sale to the holder of such bonds and coupons as his ratable share of such net proceeds after allowing for the proportion of the total purchase price required to pay the various expenses, charges and other items, which, as provided in the last preceding section, are to be deducted from the gross proceeds of sale before applying any of such proceeds upon the bonds or appurtenant coupons; and such purchaser shall be credited, on account of the purchase price of the property purchased, with the sums payable out of such net proceeds on the bonds and coupons so turned in, and, at any such sale, any holder of bonds or their agents may bid for and purchase such property and may make payment therefor as aforesaid, and, upon compliance with the terms of sale, may hold, retain and dispose of such property without further accountability therefor.

 Section 2. While in possession of the mortgaged premises the company shall also have full power, in its discretion, from time to time, to dispose, free from the lien of this indenture, of any portion of the implements, machinery, patterns or equipment embraced within this indenture which may have become unfit for use or undesirable and, if the same is not replaced by new implements, machinery or equipment, of at least equal value to that disposed of, the proceeds of sale shall be deposited with the trustee and paid out the same as other funds coming into the possession of the trustee. 

Section 3. In no event shall any purchaser or purchasers of any property sold or disposed of under any provision of this article be required to see to the application of the purchase money.

Section 4. In case the mortgaged premises shall be in the possession of a receiver lawfully appointed, the powers in and by this article conferred upon the company may be exercised by such receiver, with the approval of the trustee; and, if the trustee shall be in possession of the mortgaged premises under any provisions of this indenture, then all the powers by this article conferred upon the company may be exercised by the trustee in its discretion:

Section 5. A certificate of the company under its corporate seal signed and verified by the affidavit of its president or a vice-president may be received by the trustee as conclusive evidence of any of the statements therein set forth, and shall be full warrant to the trustee for any action taken or suffered by it under the provisions of this article on the faith thereof; but in its discretion the trustee may require such further or additional evidence as to it may seem reasonable. If the trustee shall determine to make any further inquiry or require further or additional evidence, it may examine the books, records and premises of the company personally or by its agents or attorneys. The expenses of any such examination shall be paid by the company and if not so paid by it, the said expenses and any amount 524

FORMS 

[No. 76 advanced by the trustee in payment or part payment thereof, together with interest thereon at the rate of six per cent per annum shall be paid in full out of the trust estate prior to any payment therefrom of or on account of the bonds and coupons issued hereunder. 

Section 6. Nothing shall be done under this article if the result thereof would be in any way prejudicially to affect the bonds hereby secured as a legal investment for savings banks under the laws of the state of Michigan. 

Article VI. 

Concerning Bondholders. 

Section 1. Any request, direction or other instrument required by this indenture to be signed and executed by bondholders, may be in any number of concurrent writings of similar tenor, and may be signed or executed by such bondholders in person or by attorney appointed in writing or by a committee constituted by an agreement to which any portion of the bonds shall have been made subject by deposit or otherwise. Proof of the execution of such request, direction or other instrument, or of the writing appointing any such agent, and of the ownership of bonds, if made in the following manner, shall be sufficient for any purpose of this indenture, and shall be conclusive in favor of the trustee with regard to action by it taken under such request, to-wit: (a) The fact and date of the execution by any person of any such writing may be proved by the certificate of any officer in any jurisdiction, who, by the laws thereof, has power to take affidavits within said jurisdiction, certifying that the persons signing such writing did acknowledge before him the execution thereof or by an affidavit of a witness to such execution duly sworn to before such officer. (b) The fact of the holding of bonds hereunder by any bondholder, and the amount and numbers of any such bonds, and the date of his holding the same, may be proved by a certificate executed by any trust com- 525

No. 76]  

pany, bank, bankers, or other depository, if such certificate shall be deemed by the trustee to be satisfactory, showing that at the date therein mentioned such persons had on deposit with such trust company, bank, bankers or other depository the bonds described in such certificate. The trustee may deem that bonds mentioned in any such certificate continue to be held as stated therein until the trustee shall receive notice to the contrary evidenced by certificate similarly executed. The ownership of bonds which have been registered shall be proved by the books of the registrar of said bonds.

Article VII. 

Concerning the Trustee. 

Section 1. The trustee, or any successor or successors hereafter appointed, may resign and be discharged of the trusts hereby created by written notice to the company, mailed to the company at its address as furnished to said trustee, thirty days prior to the date upon which such resignation shall take effect, and upon due execution and delivery of a proper instrument or instruments of transfer of the trust to its successor or successors in trust.

FORMS 

[No. 76 the said appointment shall, at the expiration of said thirty days, be considered as assented to and confirmed by the holders of the bonds secured hereby. In case such objection by the holders of a majority in amount of said bonds shall be made as aforesaid, the company shall thereupon apply to some court of competent jurisdiction to appoint instead such trustee as to such court shall seem meet. At least ten days' notice of such publication shall be given by mail to said objecting bondholders at the addresses stated as aforesaid. 

Section 3. Any trustee appointed in either of the methods aforesaid shall, from the time of appointment and acceptance, have possession of and be vested with the same rights and powers as trustee, as it would have had, possessed and been vested with, had it originally been made a party to this instrument.

Section 4. The trustee shall not be precluded from underwriting, guaranteeing the subscription of, or subscribing for the whole or any part of the bonds secured hereby for a commission or other remuneration, or from purchasing, holding, dealing in, and disposing of the bonds or any part thereof, or from otherwise at any time contracting or entering into any financial or other transaction with the company, or being interested in any such contract or transaction, and the trustee shall not be in any wise liable to account, either to the company, or to the bondholders, for any profits made thereby or in connection therewith.

Section 5. The trustee may at any time accept any conveyance, mortgage, assignment or transfer of any property, real or personal, which any person or corporation may make and deliver to said trustee, as a further security for the bonds issued or to be issued hereunder, and the property so conveyed, mortgaged, assigned or transferred, if and when the conveyance, mortgage, assignment or transfer thereof shall be accepted by the trustee shall thereupon become further security as aforesaid, but the trustee may at any time in its absolute and uncontrolled discretion release any such further security. 527

No. 76] 

Section 6. The trustee, for itself and its successors, hereby accepts the trust and assumes the duties hereby created and imposed, upon and only upon the following terms and conditions, to-wit: 

1. The recitals of fact herein contained and contained in the bonds hereby executed or intended so to be shall be taken as statements made by the company, and shall not be construed as made by the trustee. 

2. It shall be no part of the duty of the trustee to record or file these presents as a mortgage of real or chattel property or to do any other act for the continuance of the lien of this indenture, or to give notice of the existence of the lien thereof, or to extend or supplement the lien sought to be created hereby; nor shall it be any part of the duty of the trustee to pay or keep itself advised as to the payment of insurance premiums, taxes, assessments or other obligations of or upon the trust estate, or to require the payment of such insurance premiums, taxes, assessments or other obligations, or to effect insurance upon the same or any part thereof, but the company shall and will do all things needful in that behalf. The trustee may, however, in its discretion, at the expense of the company, do any or all of the matters or things in this paragraph set forth, or require the same to be done. 

3. The trustee may select and employ in and about said trusts and duties suitable agents and attorneys, whose reasonable compensation shall be paid by the company, or in default of such payment, shall be a charge upon the trust estate and the proceeds thereof paramount to said bonds and the trustee shall not be liable for any neglect, omission or wrong-doing of any such agents or attorneys, reasonable care being exercised in their selection. 

4. The trustee shall not be liable for the exercise of any discretion or power hereunder or mistakes or errors in judgment or otherwise in connection with this trust except for its own wilful misconduct or gross negligence. 

5. The trustee shall have a first lien upon the mortgaged premises and the proceeds thereof for its reason- 528

FORMS 

[No. 76 able expenses, counsel fees and compensation incurred in the performance of said trust powers and duties, and the company agrees to pay the same. 

6. The trustee shall be under no obligation or duty to perform any act hereunder or to institute or defend any suit in respect thereof, unless properly indemnified to its satisfaction. The trustee shall not be required to ascertain or to inquire as to the performance of any of the covenants or agreements on the part of the company, and it shall not be deemed to have knowledge of any default of the company hereunder and it may conclusively assume that there has been no such default unless and until it shall have been specifically notified in writing of such default by the company or the holders of not less than twenty-five per cent (25%) in amount, of the bonds then outstanding hereunder. Except as herein otherwise expressly provided the trustee shall not be bound to recognize any person as the holder of a bond issued hereunder unless and until his bond is submitted to the trustee for inspection, if required, and his title thereto satisfactorily established if disputed. 

7. The exclusive right of action hereunder shall be vested in the trustee, until refusal of the trustee so to act, and no bondholder shall have a right to enforce these presents, until after demand made upon the trustee, accompanied by a tender of indemnity satisfactory to it as aforesaid and refusal of the trustee to act in accordance with said demand. 

8. The trustee shall be protected in acting upon any notice, resolution, vote, request, consent, certificate, affidavit, voucher, bond or other paper or document, believed by it to be genuine and to be passed or signed by the proper party.
